documents.t: The folder Decision-Definitions contains a definition per decision model, each packaged so that it can be deployed using the SAS Container Runtime (SCR). More on the SCR in the SAS Documentation.

A decision model (a System One model, the category TypeSafe's Jev established) does not generate text. It takes a state - a ticket, a record, a document, as text or as a JSON object - and one or more typed questions, and returns a calibrated answer per question: Question type Asks Answer choice Which one of these options? the chosen option, a probability per option, a confidence noul Does this condition hold? the probability that it does score Where on this ordered scale? the probability-weighted position, a probability per level, a confidence Every question in one call is evaluated against the same state, so ten questions cost one state upload. A call takes around a second and, for a hosted model, a fraction of the token price of a chat completion. The model returns no reasoning: where a human needs an explanation, pair it with an LLM. It is also weak on numbers and dates - keep those in rules. This is the shape a SAS Intelligent Decisioning branch node wants: a value to branch on and a confidence to gate it with. Typical uses are ticket and document routing, escalation and risk flags, screening an input for prompt injection before an LLM call, and reranking retrieved chunks.

Inputs: state, questions (the question map in the System One shape, as a JSON string) and options ({key:value,...}; API_KEY for a hosted model). Outputs: answers (the whole answer map as JSON), answer and confidence (the first question's headline answer - the chosen option, the score, or yes/no for a noul), run_time, prompt_length and output_length (always 0). A single-question call therefore needs no parsing in the decision flow: branch on answer, and route the case to a person or an LLM when confidence is below the threshold you validated on your own labelled cases. Several questions come back together in answers. {"inputs": [ {"name": "state", "value": "Hi, I was charged twice for my March invoice. Please refund one payment."}, {"name": "questions", "value": "{\"team\": {\"type\": \"choice\", \"instructions\": \"Which team handles this?\", \"criteria\": {\"billing\": \"payments and refunds\", \"technical\": \"bugs and outages\", \"sales\": \"pricing and upgrades\"}}}"}, {"name": "options", "value": "{API_KEY:sk-...}"} ]}

Definition Model Where it runs Key jev_1_13 Jev 1.13 by TypeSafe OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-1.13) the OpenRouter entry of the credential domain clef_flash Clef-flash by Cloudflare (Apache-2.0, open weights) - the most accurate measured on many-option intent sets OpenRouter (cloudflare/clef-flash) the OpenRouter entry liquid_d1 Liquid D1 by Liquid AI - the cheapest hosted decision model measured OpenRouter (liquid/d1) the OpenRouter entry pplx_decider_27b Perplexity Decider 27B - a 256k context OpenRouter (perplexity/pplx-decider-v1-27b) the OpenRouter entry mercury_decide Mercury Decide by Inception - a 65,536-token context; not measured yet, so its model card has no Evaluation section OpenRouter (inception/mercury-decide) the OpenRouter entry von_1_2 Von 1.2 (Apache-2.0, ModernBERT-large) inside the container, checkpoint staged on the shared llm-weights volume none Each model card carries an Evaluation section with what was measured for the model - accuracy on hand-written cases, public datasets and the JevBench tasks, calibration error, latency, cost per 1,000 calls and one caution - from a benchmark of about 50 examples per dataset: a shortlist to start from, then measure on your own labelled cases. A definition's metadata.evaluation is that paragraph; leave it out and the card has no such section. Two more fields of a decision manifest say what the model accepts: metadata.max_options (the most options a choice question may carry; 255 unless the model takes less - Tev1 24, Solar Decide 26) and metadata.question_types (the subset of choice, noul, score it answers; Tev1 answers choices only). Both default to everything, land in the fact sheet as max_options and question_types, and are registered as the custom properties contextLength, maxOptions and questionTypes of the Model Manager model, which the Prompt Builder reads to draw its model cards and to grey out a model that cannot take the current template. Every provider in this family speaks the same wire format (POST .../v1/systemone), so the one dec_systemone_api score template also covers TypeSafe's own API (mdb add typesafe jev-latest, key entry TypeSafe from TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and any self-hosted server that copies it. Von's dec_von template loads the checkpoint at the first call a container answers and keeps it for every later call of that container; the container never contacts the Hugging Face Hub at run time, and inference runs on the CPU. The checkpoint is 3 GB - too large for the image build - so von_1_2 ships with weights_source: mounted: create the llm-weights volume and run the staging job once as described in Serving Open-Weight Models, and mdb deploy renders the persistent-volume variant for it.

Decision models are registered and published with the same mdb command line as the LLMs - see Register & Publish LLMs for register, publish, --update, --wait and ship. They land in the Decision Model Project of the LLM repository, which mdb register (or mdb setup) creates when it is missing. mdb register jev_1_13 von_1_2 mdb publish jev_1_13 von_1_2 --wait mdb deploy jev_1_13 von_1_2 --registry <your-registry> # the SCR deployment YAML, then kubectl apply mdb add openrouter <model> --kind decision, mdb add typesafe jev-latest and mdb add von create new decision definitions; OpenRouter's public model listing omits its decision models, so the bundled catalog snapshot supplies them (Jev, Mercury Decide, Clef and Clef-flash, Liquid D1, Perplexity Decider, Kev, Tev1, Solar Decide) and marks them as decision models: mdb add openrouter inception/mercury-decide --id mercury_decide --yes builds a decision definition. A decision model the snapshot does not know needs --kind decision, or it becomes a chat LLM. mdb test <id> runs the generated scorer on a support ticket with all three question types, and mdb load-facts - or the Load-Fact-Sheets.sas program - loads the DECISION_FACT_SHEET table beside the LLM and embedding fact sheets. In the Prompt Builder a decision template (one of the kinds offered on the Setup card, under What are you building?) lists the models of the Decision Model Project, replaces the two prompts with a state template and a question designer, checks runs against expected answers, evaluates them over labelled cases and manifests typed outputs - see Decision templates in the User Guide. The project is found by its name, so no report option names it. The kind as a whole has a switch among the options of the Prompt Builder object, Enable decision templates (enableDecision), which is Enabled by default: a site that publishes no decision models sets it to Disabled, and the Prompt Builder then offers no decision kind, does not look the project up and calls no decision model - see Deploying the Builder UIs.

This page details considerations when deploying the decisions in MAS/SCR. Every prompt template checks for an environment variable called LLMCONTAINERPATH. If this variable does not exist it will default to the value that was provided as an endpoint for the LLM Prompt Builder where that prompt template was created. Setting this environment variable will enable you to deploy the same decision across multiple environments and also changing the LLM endpoints in case you have fully isolated environments.

If a prompt was manifested with the Include the LLM call in the manifested model option, the generated Python model performs the LLM call itself using the requests package — a requirements.json is stored with the model so publishing destinations that build a Python environment install it. A manifested decision template always calls its decision model this way. In addition to LLMCONTAINERPATH, these models check three more environment variables: LLMCONTAINERCABUNDLE: path to the CA bundle used to verify the TLS connection to the LLM container. It defaults to /security/trustedcerts.pem. SAS Viya mounts that file into the pods of CAS and of the compute servers, so a model that runs there — the in-app test of SAS Intelligent Decisioning, a SAS Studio session — verifies an ingress secured by the deployment's own CA without any setting. The file is not in every container that runs Python: where SAS Micro Analytic Service runs Python in a separate runner container, it is missing there — see Publishing to SAS Micro Analytic Service: the certificate bundle. When the file does not exist, the model verifies against the public certificate authorities that come with requests, and a certificate signed by the deployment's own CA is then refused. LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY: switches TLS verification on or off for this destination, whatever the model was manifested with. false, no or 0 switches it off; true, yes or 1 switches it on. Upper and lower case are the same. When the variable is not set, or holds any other word, the model does what was written into it when it was manifested — see the default written at manifest time. LLMCONTAINERTIMEOUT: timeout for the LLM call in seconds (default 600). If the LLM call fails (network issue, TLS failure or a non-200 response), the model does not raise an error — the failure message is returned in the response output, the parsed output variables keep their default values and parse_status returns 0. A decision template returns the message in its answer output, and its other outputs stay empty.
documents.s: Prompt templates with the included LLM call

documents.t: The Options pane of the Prompt Builder has the checkbox Verify TLS certificates in manifested models (sslVerify, ticked by default — see the options of the Prompt Builder). Its state is written into the score code of every model manifested from then on: The option when the model was manifested LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY on the destination The model ticked not set, or another word verifies — against the bundle, or against the public CAs when the bundle file is missing ticked false, no, 0 does not verify not ticked not set, or another word does not verify not ticked true, yes, 1 verifies, as in the first row Three things follow from that: The option is a default for new manifests. A model that is already manifested keeps what it was manifested with until it is manifested again; changing the option changes no registered model and no published one. The environment variable wins in both directions, so a model manifested with verification off can be made to verify on one destination, and the reverse, without manifesting it again. With the option ticked, a model behaves as a model manifested before release 2.3.0 does. The option reaches the models that make an HTTPS call themselves: a prompt template with the included LLM call, a decision template, and the retrieval model of a RAG setup, which reads two variables of its own — see RAG Ingestion and Retrieval. A retrieval model registered with the SAS Studio custom step RAG - Register Setup is not manifested in the Prompt Builder and does not get the option: the step has a checkbox of its own, Verify TLS certificates in the registered retrieval model, which writes the same default — see the checkbox of the custom step. The option does not change a prompt manifested for the Call LLM node, where the node makes the call, nor anything the Prompt Builder page does in the browser, nor the ingestion job of a RAG setup.
documents.s: The default written at manifest time

documents.t: A model manifested while the option was not ticked carries the tag TLS-Verification-Off in SAS Model Manager: a decision template, the retrieval model of a RAG setup, and a prompt template manifested with the included LLM call. The step that manifests it shows a warning before the button is clicked — Finalize for a decision template, Finalize for a prompt only while Include the LLM call in the manifested model is ticked, and Manifest setup for a RAG setup. A retrieval model registered with the custom step RAG - Register Setup while its checkbox Verify TLS certificates in the registered retrieval model is not ticked carries the same tag, and the log of the step ends with WARNING lines that say so. A prompt manifested for the Call LLM node makes no call itself, so it gets neither the warning nor the tag. The tag stands with the model's other tags, such as LLM-Call-Included. To list every such model, filter the models on that tag in SAS Model Manager, or ask the model repository: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ "https://<sas-viya-host>/modelRepository/models?filter=contains(tags,'TLS-Verification-Off')&limit=100" \ | jq -r '.items[] | [.name, .projectName, .modifiedBy] | @tsv' The tag says what the model was manifested with, not what a destination does: LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY=true on a destination makes a tagged model verify there, and LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY=false stops an untagged one from verifying. Manifesting the model again with the option ticked removes the tag, on all three kinds; running the custom step again with its checkbox ticked removes it from a model the step registered. The tag follows the score code the model holds, with one case the page cannot decide. A manifest whose score code SAS Model Manager refused is reported as failed and leaves the tags as they were. When the upload of the score code gets no answer at all — the connection drops, or an ingress answers with its error page — SAS Model Manager may have stored the code all the same; the manifest then says beside its button that it is not known whether the score code was stored, leaves the tags as they were and asks for the manifest to be repeated. Until a manifest of that model completes, its tag may not match its score code, in either direction; the line in the score code named below is what counts. The tags are the first thing written once the score code is stored, before requirements.json and the attributes of the model, so a manifest of a prompt or decision template that stops at a later request — The manifest was not completed beside its button — leaves the tags of the score code that is stored. When the tags could not be updated, the manifest says so beside its button in both directions — the tag could not be written to a model that does not verify, or could not be taken away from one that does — so that it can be put right in SAS Model Manager. To read the setting in the score code itself, open the model in SAS Model Manager and look for one line. The score code of a prompt template with the included LLM call and of a decision template holds sslVerifyDefault = True or sslVerifyDefault = False. The retrieve_context.py of a retrieval model holds SSL_VERIFY = True or SSL_VERIFY = False in its MANIFEST block. A prompt manifested for the Call LLM node holds neither line. Nothing else in the score code of a prompt or decision template carries the name sslVerifyDefault: the Prompt Builder refuses a variable, an output variable or a question of that name.
documents.s: Finding the models that do not verify

documents.t: Please note that it is not supported to change the type of deployment between environments so if you have the LLM containers deployed in Kubernetes in one environment, they will have to be deployed in the same fashion in all other environments as well. If you have selected a Kubernetes based deployment set the variable value to the corresponding of this: https://base-url/llm. If you have selected an Azure Container Apps/Instaces based deployment set the variable value to the corresponding value of this: randomString.region.azurecontainerapps.io from the https://model.randomString.region.azurecontainerapps.io/model URL.

Please note that you do not have to set this environment variable if you are ok with utilizing the hardcoded value provided by LLM Prompt Builder. If you are deploying the decisions to a SCR destination than just add the LLMCONTAINERPATH environment variable as part of the env definition in the YAML file. That means you can give every instance potentially a different endpoint! If you are deploying the decisions to MAS you will have to add the LLMCONTAINERPATH environment variable to the sas-microanalytic-score pod via a PatchTransformer. That means you can only have one instance of this per MAS deployment and if it is set once it will apply to all. Here is an example of a PatchTransformer: apiVersion: builtin kind: PatchTransformer metadata: name: mas-llm-transformer patch: |- # Add LLM environment variable - op: add path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/- value: name: LLMCONTAINERPATH value: <YOURVALUE> target: group: apps kind: Deployment name: sas-microanalytic-score version: v1 This transformer adds the variable to the first container of the pod, the main container sas-microanalytic-score. Every prompt template reads LLMCONTAINERPATH in its Python score code, with or without the included LLM call: a prompt manifested for the Call LLM node builds the URL it hands to the node in that code too. Where MAS runs Python in a separate runner container, the score code does not run in the first container — set the variable on the runner as well, as the variable and the Python runner below shows.

A decision references a custom node by its id, not by its name: the step of the node holds the address /decisions/decisionNodeTypes/<id>, and the code of the node is read from that address every time the decision is tested, its code is generated or it is published. A transfer package of a folder with a decision carries the node it uses, with its id, and an import matches the node by that id alone. Where every site creates the node under an id of its own, a decision built on one site does not find its node on another. The accelerator therefore ships the Call LLM node under one id, f9efcbb7-f57b-4a62-b56d-1a89595e2039. The content folder holds the decision Decisions/Call LLM Node, which uses only this node and is not meant to be published: the transfer package carries the node under that id as its dependency, and a decision built with it on one site imports on another without a mapping.
documents.s: The Call LLM node and its id

documents.t: The import of the package creates the node under the id, with the content of the release: mdb builders-import imports the decision and the node type in a transfer job of their own - see Install or upgrade with the transfer package. On a site that has the node under that id already, the import overwrites it in place - its code and its terms become the ones of the release, and local edits of them are gone -, also where the node was made on the site by the program below or by the migration. Or run Create-Custom-SAS-Intelligent-Decisioning-Node.sas (folder SAS-Intelligent-Decisioning-Integration). It creates the node under the id. It asks for the id first and creates nothing where the node is there already: the log then names Update-Custom-SAS-Intelligent-Decisioning-Node.sas, which brings the content of the node to the one of the release. It creates nothing either where a node named Call LLM is there under another id, and its ERROR lines name the migration below. It never sends the request that creates a node for an id that is taken: SAS Viya answers such a request with an error, and renames the node of that id to the name of the request before it does. Update-Custom-SAS-Intelligent-Decisioning-Node.sas looks for the node under the id first. Where no node is there, it updates the node named Call LLM and says in a NOTE that the node of the site is not under the shipped id yet.

A site that created the node with the program of an earlier release has it under an id of its own. A node cannot be given another id, and node names are unique, so the node of the release cannot be created beside it. Run the migration once, before the import: mdb decision-node-migrate # dry run: the node and every decision version that calls it - changes nothing mdb decision-node-migrate --apply mdb builders-import With --apply the command: renames the node of the site to Call LLM (before f9efcbb7), so that its name is free; creates Call LLM under the shipped id, with the settings, the code and the terms of the node of the site; moves every decision that calls the old node to the new one, by a transfer re-import of the decision over itself with a mapping of the node from the old id to the new one. This rewrites every version of the decision, the locked ones included, and keeps the ids of the versions. An edit in SAS Intelligent Decisioning, or a change over REST, reaches the current version only: a locked version cannot be changed any other way. The tasks of each import job are read, and every version is read back; keeps the old node. --delete-old deletes it at the end, and only when a fresh look finds no version of any decision that calls it. Published modules - in SAS Micro Analytic Service or in a SAS Container Runtime image - hold the compiled code of the decision and are not affected: they keep running as they are. A moved decision uses the new node from its next test, code generation or publish on. A run that stopped is run again: what was done is found done. A node renamed by hand. A site that renamed its old node itself, to free the name, and then imported the package or ran the Create program has the node under the shipped id and its decisions still on the old one. mdb decision-node-migrate reads every decision there as well and lists every version that calls a node like Call LLM - one with the code of the node under the shipped id, or, as a warning, one whose name starts with Call LLM and whose code is another. Check that such a node is an older Call LLM before you move its decisions. mdb decision-node-migrate --from-id <id of the old node> --apply moves the decisions of that node to the one under the shipped id; it creates and renames nothing. With --delete-old it deletes that node only when it is a copy. A node with other code is kept, and the run says so: delete it in SAS Intelligent Decisioning once you are sure. Never delete a node that a decision uses. SAS Viya does not refuse the delete. It removes the reference to the node from every version of every decision that uses it, the locked ones included: their tests fail with customObjectURI is null, and their code cannot be generated. Creating a node under the old id again does not bring the reference back - there is no undo. The dry run of the migration lists such versions as a warning. A transfer re-import of each decision with a mapping to an existing node is the only repair. Moving the Call LLM node to its id lists the options of the command.
documents.s: A site that has the node under another id

documents.t: mdb builders-import asks the site before it uploads anything of the decisions. Where a node named Call LLM is there under another id, it leaves the decision and the node out, imports the rest of the package, and ends with exit code 1 and the migration command; --no-decisions leaves them out on purpose. A transfer import of the package by other means - in SAS Environment Manager, or with the transfer service directly - goes ahead: the task of the node fails with Decision node type names must be unique (409), and the decision of the same package is skipped without a task of its own, while the import job still ends completed. Read the tasks of such a job, not only its state, and run the migration before the import. Measured on 2026-10-20 on the test system with nodes and decisions of a test, not with Call LLM: the creation under a chosen id, the rename that a create request for a taken id caused, the delete that cleared the reference in a locked version and the re-import that repaired it, the unaffected MAS module, and the failed import with its skipped decision. A decision moved by the re-import was then checked in SAS Intelligent Decisioning: its current and its locked version ran with the new node. Measured on 2026-10-21: the import of a package over a node of the same id whose content was made on the site - as the Create program and the migration make it - completed, gave the node the code and the terms of the package, and the decision of the package ran with it.
documents.s: Importing the package on such a site

documents.t: A decision that works in the in-app test of SAS Intelligent Decisioning can fail with a certificate error once it is published to SAS Micro Analytic Service (MAS). The in-app test runs in CAS, where the CA bundle is mounted. MAS can run Python in a container where it is not. What follows was measured on one deployment (SAS Viya on Kubernetes, namespace viya4). Container and volume names can differ on yours, so the steps start with a command that shows what you have.
documents.s: Publishing to SAS Micro Analytic Service: the certificate bundle

documents.t: The deployment sas-microanalytic-score has two containers: sas-microanalytic-score and a Python runner, there named viya4-mas-python-runner — the name carries the deployment's name prefix. The pod has a volume named security, an emptyDir that the init container sas-certframe fills. It holds the trust bundle trustedcerts.pem, and more than that: the private key directory of the pod, private, is in the same volume. The main container mounts the whole volume at /security, and parts of it a second time elsewhere by subPath (cacerts, private). It has SSLCALISTLOC=/security/trustedcerts.pem. The Python runner mounts four volumes, and security is not one of them: pytmp at /tmp, pylog at /pylog, python-volume at /opt/sas/viya/home/sas-pyconfig and astores-volume at /models/resources/viya. It has no certificate environment variable, and inside it /security/trustedcerts.pem does not exist. A manifested model that calls the model container itself runs in the Python runner. It looks for the bundle, does not find the file, falls back to the public certificate authorities, and refuses the certificate of an ingress that is signed by the deployment's own CA.

The publishing validation of the decision ends with HTTP 201, and every row carries the error in the model's text output — answer for a decision template, response for a prompt template — while the other outputs are empty: Decision model call failed: HTTPSConnectionPool(host=..., port=443): Max retries exceeded with url: /llm/von_1_2/von_1_2 (Caused by SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError(1, '[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: self-signed certificate in certificate chain'))) For a prompt template the line starts with LLM call failed:. The URL names the model container that was called, here von_1_2.

The same decision returns answers in the in-app test of SAS Intelligent Decisioning, which runs in CAS, and fails in the publishing validation on the MAS destination. A decision that reaches the same model container through the Call LLM node works on the same MAS destination. The node is DS2 code and runs in the main container, which has the bundle. The Python runner has no bundle. Find the container names, then look for the file: kubectl -n <namespace> get deployment sas-microanalytic-score -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].name}' kubectl -n <namespace> exec deploy/sas-microanalytic-score -c <prefix>-mas-python-runner -- ls -l /security/trustedcerts.pem No such file or directory is this case. If the file is listed, the cause is another one: the certificate of the endpoint is not signed by a CA in that bundle — point LLMCONTAINERCABUNDLE at a bundle that covers it.
documents.s: How to tell that it is this case

documents.t: Mount the bundle file into the Python runner. Verification stays on, and no model has to be manifested again. This is the fix for production; the steps are in the next section. Switch verification off for the models concerned: clear Verify TLS certificates in manifested models in the Options pane of the Prompt Builder and manifest the model again (for a retrieval model registered with the custom step RAG - Register Setup: clear the step's checkbox Verify TLS certificates in the registered retrieval model and run the step again), or set LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY=false on the destination (see the variable and the Python runner). Either way the model no longer checks that the answer comes from the real model container: whatever answers on that address inside the network is believed, and the prompt or the state is sent to it. That is acceptable on a test system whose cluster network is closed to others. It is not a setting for production — there, mount the bundle. On the deployment described here the option made exactly that difference: a decision whose decision template was manifested with verification off returned answers in the publishing validation on the MAS destination, and the same decision with the template manifested with verification on failed there with the error above.

The volume already exists in the pod; the runner only lacks the mount. Mount the bundle file, not the volume. The security volume also holds the private key directory of the pod — /security/private in the main container — and the runner is the container that executes the code of the models. A mount with subPath gives the runner the one file it needs and nothing else of the volume. In both forms, replace <prefix>-mas-python-runner with the container name that the first command above printed. For a test. Save the patch as mas-python-runner-trust.patch.yaml: spec: template: spec: containers: - name: <prefix>-mas-python-runner volumeMounts: - name: security mountPath: /security/trustedcerts.pem subPath: trustedcerts.pem readOnly: true Then apply it. The patch is a file because a patch written on the command line is quoted differently in PowerShell and in bash: kubectl -n <namespace> patch deployment sas-microanalytic-score --type=strategic --patch-file mas-python-runner-trust.patch.yaml The patch changes the pod template, so it restarts the MAS pods — plan it like any other restart of MAS. A one-off patch is also overwritten by the next update of the deployment, which is why the second form exists. To see what the patch does before anything changes, add --dry-run=client -o yaml to the command. On the deployment this was written against, that dry run added the mount to the runner and left the main container as it was. To keep it. Add the same patch, with the header kustomize needs, to the site configuration of the deployment, for example as site-config/sas-microanalytic-score/mas-python-runner-trust.yaml: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: sas-microanalytic-score spec: template: spec: containers: - name: <prefix>-mas-python-runner volumeMounts: - name: security mountPath: /security/trustedcerts.pem subPath: trustedcerts.pem readOnly: true List it under patches: in kustomization.yaml: patches: - path: site-config/sas-microanalytic-score/mas-python-runner-trust.yaml target: kind: Deployment name: sas-microanalytic-score Then build and apply the deployment as your site normally does. Check the result after either form, once the rollout has ended. On the deployment described here the form for a test was applied on 2026-10-11 by the owner of the cluster, with the patch and the command as they stand above: The deployment rolled to a new pod, and that pod became ready with both containers (2/2). In the runner, ls -l /security then listed exactly one entry, trustedcerts.pem (367,876 bytes). The directory private of the volume was not visible there. A decision whose decision template is manifested with verification on — its score code holds sslVerifyDefault = True and passes verify=sslVerify to the call — was published again to the MAS destination maslocal with Replace item with the same name. Its publishing validation ended with Completed successfully on four rows: four answers with HTTP status 201 and an empty error column. Before the patch the same decision had answered CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED there. A second decision, with three model nodes that were all manifested in the Prompt Builder — the retrieval model of a RAG setup, a prompt template with the included LLM call and a decision template — was published to maslocal the same day, with the bundle mounted and verification on. All three nodes ran; its publishing validation ended on three rows with HTTP status 201 and an empty error column, and the prompt template and the decision template answered. The retrieval model answered retrieval failed: RuntimeError: no vector-store credentials resolved: … in retrieval_status, with no chunk: the runner had no PGVECTOR_RAG_USER and PGVECTOR_RAG_PW. The retrieval model in a decision names the variables it needs. The same decision with the user and the password of the vector store passed per call, in the options input of the retrieval model: called one row at a time, six calls one after another each returned HTTP status 201, retrieval_status ok, three hits, an envelope of 1969 characters and the answer of the LLM from the retrieved context — with verification on in the score code of all three models. Its publishing validation on maslocal gave different results from run to run: all three rows complete in one, and in others rows with HTTP status 201, an empty error column and empty outputs of every node. That was not the certificate, and not the lengths of the model's variables: SAS Micro Analytic Service had ended those executions after 30 seconds, because the validation sends its rows at the same time and the two self-hosted models behind the nodes then took longer than that (the execution timed out). The same decision with PGVECTOR_RAG_USER and PGVECTOR_RAG_PW as environment variables: set on the containers of the deployment from a Kubernetes secret (kubectl set env deployment/sas-microanalytic-score --containers=* --from=secret/<name>; the pod restarts), a call with {} as the options of the retrieval model returned retrieval_status ok and three hits. Which of the containers needs the two variables was not separated. That was the one-off patch, not the kustomize form: on that deployment the mount is lost at the next apply of the deployment unless the kustomize form is added. Not measured: the kustomize form itself on a cluster; the call of a retrieval model to the SAS Viya credentials service from SAS Micro Analytic Service, which it does not make when the credentials come with the call or from the environment; the credentials of the vector store as environment variables in the test of SAS Intelligent Decisioning and in a SAS Container Runtime container; and whether a variable set on the main container alone reaches the Python in the runner, which the variable and the Python runner is about. Container and volume names can differ on your deployment, so the check stays part of the procedure. kubectl -n <namespace> rollout status deployment sas-microanalytic-score kubectl -n <namespace> exec deploy/sas-microanalytic-score -c <prefix>-mas-python-runner -- ls -l /security/trustedcerts.pem kubectl -n <namespace> exec deploy/sas-microanalytic-score -c <prefix>-mas-python-runner -- ls /security The first ls has to list the file. The second should show that file and nothing else — no private directory. Then run the publishing validation of the decision again: the rows have to carry answers instead of the error. If the file is listed and an error stays, read its text again — a different text is a different cause.
documents.s: Mounting the bundle into the Python runner

documents.t: A Python model reads the environment of the container its code runs in. That holds for every LLMCONTAINER... variable: LLMCONTAINERPATH, which every prompt template and every decision template reads, and LLMCONTAINERCABUNDLE, LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY and LLMCONTAINERTIMEOUT, which the models that make the call themselves read. The PatchTransformer in MAS vs SCR adds a variable to the first container of the pod, which on the deployment described here is the main one and not the runner. The containers of a pod do not share their environment, and whether MAS hands the environment of its main container on to the Python it starts in the runner has not been measured. So where MAS runs Python in a separate runner, add the variable to the runner as well, by its name, and look at what the runner really has with the command below: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: sas-microanalytic-score spec: template: spec: containers: - name: <prefix>-mas-python-runner env: - name: LLMCONTAINERPATH value: <YOURVALUE> It is listed under patches: like the mount above. Another variable is another entry of the same env list — LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY with the value "false", in quotes, for the second of the two ways out; the RAGEMBED_... and RAGSTORE_... variables of a retrieval model go there in the same way, and so do the user and the password of its vector store, PGVECTOR_RAG_USER and PGVECTOR_RAG_PW for pgvector — a retrieval model without them answers no vector-store credentials resolved and returns no chunk (the retrieval model in a decision has the full list). A password in the env of a deployment is readable by everyone who can read the deployment; a Kubernetes secret referenced with valueFrom keeps it out of the manifest. Measured on 2026-10-11 for the two variables of the vector store: taken from a Kubernetes secret and set on every container of the deployment with kubectl set env deployment/sas-microanalytic-score --containers=* --from=secret/<name>, after which the pod restarted, they reached the retrieval model — a call with {} as its options returned retrieval_status ok and three hits. That was every container at once, so it does not say which of them needs the variables. Check it like the mount, with env in place of ls: kubectl -n <namespace> exec deploy/sas-microanalytic-score -c <prefix>-mas-python-runner -- env The output has to hold the variable with your value (pipe it through grep LLMCONTAINER, or Select-String LLMCONTAINER in PowerShell, to shorten it). A variable set this way holds for every model published to that MAS — LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY=false, for one, also for the models manifested with verification on.
documents.s: The variable and the Python runner

documents.t: This step is optional. With it, the LLM Prompt Builder gains an Optimize section that improves a prompt automatically with DSPy: a SAS Job Execution job rewrites nothing by hand — it uses the experiment runs the prompt engineer marked as Best Response (or a governed CAS table) as training data, runs an optimizer (bootstrap few-shot; MIPROv2, which also rewrites the instruction; or GEPA, which evolves it from natural-language feedback) against a metric (exact match, token-overlap F1 or an LLM judge), and records the result on the prompt itself for the user to review, judge and accept. Nothing is ever applied automatically. The feature is off by default. It is switched on with Enable prompt optimization (DSPy) (enableOptimization), one of the three switches among the options of the Prompt Builder object — the other two, for decision templates and for RAG setups, are independent of it. The switch is a checkbox; while it is not ticked the Optimize step is not shown and nothing is requested for it. Enabling it takes four steps: Prepare a compute context that runs as the requesting user and whose Python has dspy — the key prerequisite. Import the optimize job definition. Provide the provider keys via the credential domain (only needed for hosted models that require keys). Set the Prompt Builder Options.

The SAS Compute context the job runs in must run its sessions as the user who starts the job. The job resolves the provider keys from the credential domain and writes its result to the prompt in SAS Model Manager with the identity of its session. A context that runs its servers under a service account resolves the keys as that account and writes as that account, which may not change the prompt of a user. Whether a context does is its attribute runServerAs, which the answer of GET /compute/contexts/<id> holds as attributes.runServerAs. A context without the attribute runs as the requesting user. On SAS Viya 2026.09 the stock SAS Job Execution compute context has runServerAs set to a service account (sas-be-sa), and SAS Studio compute context has none (read on 2026-10-20). Measured on 2026-10-20 on SAS Viya 2026.09, with the job of the Prompt Builder in the SAS Job Execution compute context, before the check below: a target model with a provider key failed for want of the key, The job resolved the domain as identity sas.compute; a target model without one made all 19 model calls of the optimization and was then refused the upload of its result with HTTP 403. In the SAS Studio compute context the same run completed and wrote its result to the prompt. Granting the credential to the service account is therefore no remedy: the write to the prompt is still refused (see Managing Credentials). From release 2.3.0 the job checks both before its first model call and ends with a message when either fails: It compares the user its session runs as with the user who started the job, as Start Here and Load-Accelerator-Tables do. When the two differ the message names both, and the account as SAS Viya sees it, and says to point Optimization: compute context at a context that runs as the user who starts the job, such as SAS Studio compute context. It adds a small file, Prompt-Optimization-Write-Check.json, to the prompt and removes it again — the two requests the write of the result makes. When SAS Model Manager refuses either, the message says so with the HTTP status. The links of the model do not tell: on 2026-10-20 the session of the service account got the same update and addContent links of the model as its owner. The check is a real write: it changes the prompt's modified time, and where SAS Model Manager refuses the removal, Prompt-Optimization-Write-Check.json stays on the prompt and the message says so. Measured on 2026-10-20 on SAS Viya 2026.09 with the program of this release, against a prompt-test of five runs and the key-less target qwen_25_05b: in the SAS Job Execution compute context the job ended after 5 seconds with The optimization job runs as sas (to SAS Viya: sas.compute), not as …, who started it: the compute context SAS Job Execution compute context does not run as the user who starts the job. Point the option Optimization: compute context …, with no other milestone and no file written. In a test copy whose comparison of the two users was taken out, the same context got to the second check and ended with … may not write to the prompt … in SAS Model Manager as sas.compute: adding a file to it was answered with HTTP 403 (Forbidden). In the SAS Studio compute context the run completed - 12 model calls, the result on the prompt, and no Prompt-Optimization-Write-Check.json left on it. Not measured: a user who may read a prompt-test and not change it, and a refused removal of the file. The job runs DSPy inside proc python, so the context must also have a Python environment with the packages from SAS-Viya-Integrations/Prompt-Optimization/requirements.txt installed: dspy>=3.2.1 requests>=2.31 optuna>=3.0 Install them into the Python environment your compute contexts use — the same one configured for proc python via PROC_PYPATH, see Configuring SAS Viya for Python Integration — for example: pip install "dspy>=3.2.1" "requests>=2.31" "optuna>=3.0" optuna is only needed for the MIPROv2 optimizer (dspy treats it as an optional extra, so a plain dspy install does not pull it in — verified live). Without it, bootstrap few-shot still works and the job fails a MIPROv2 run fast with a clear message. The GEPA optimizer needs no extra package: its engine (gepa) is a hard dependency of dspy ≥ 3.2.1 and installs with it. The most common failure A compute context whose Python lacks dspy — or carries one older than 3.2.1, the version the job's DSPy adapter is validated against — is the most common reason an optimization fails. The job checks both at startup and fails fast; the message ("…lacks the dspy package" or "dspy X is too old") appears directly in the Prompt Builder's Optimize panel and in the run's optimization-tracker entry. If you see it, install/upgrade the requirements in that context's Python or point the Prompt Builder at a context that has them. Because not every deployment wants DSPy in its default environment, the context is configurable: you can prepare a dedicated context (for example Prompt Optimization — DSPy) that runs as the requesting user, with a Python environment that has the packages, and point the Prompt Builder at it. Size the context generously — an optimization run makes many model calls and runs for several minutes. Install centrally — this is an administrator task sas-pyconfig-managed environments are mounted read-only in compute pods, so the packages cannot be (and should not be) installed from a compute session — a user-level pip install will fail by design. The packages belong in the centrally managed Python configuration: add the entries from requirements.txt to the pip_installed_packages option of the target environment (e.g. default_py) in the sas-pyconfig configuration and re-run the sas-pyconfig job — see Managing Python Packages with sas-pyconfig and, for the overall proc python setup, Configuring SAS Viya for Python Integration. This keeps every compute pod consistent, survives updates and re-provisioning, and keeps package governance where it belongs. Avoid ad-hoc alternatives such as PYTHONPATH overlays on shared storage — they bypass the managed environment and are easy to leave behind unmaintained.

The job program is SAS-Viya-Integrations/Prompt-Optimization/Optimize-Prompt-DSPy.sas. Create a SAS Job Execution job definition from it: Open SAS Job Execution (/SASJobExecution/manage) and create a new job definition, for example under /Public/Jobs, named Optimize-Prompt-DSPy. Paste the program as the job's code. Note the job's SAS Content path (for example /Public/Jobs/Optimize-Prompt-DSPy) — that path is what the Prompt Builder's optimizeJobProgram Option points at. The job definition holds a copy of the program. The transfer package of the content folder brings a job definition Prompt Builder/Optimize-Prompt-DSPy with the program of its release - the package is compared with the repository before it ships -, so a site that imports the package creates no job definition of its own, points optimizeJobProgram at /SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/Prompt Builder/Optimize-Prompt-DSPy and gets the program of a new release with the import. A job definition you created by hand keeps the program of the day it was made: after an upgrade, replace its code with Optimize-Prompt-DSPy.sas of the release. From release 2.3.0 the program puts the ERROR line of a failed run together in a variable, where it wrote the message of the run into a quoted string. Measured on 2026-10-11 on SAS Viya 2026.09, with a target model whose provider key the identity of the job does not hold: with the program of release 2.3.0 in the job definition, the log of the failing run held ERROR: Prompt optimization failed: The model gpt_41_mini needs an API key for provider OpenAI but the credential domain provided none …, typed as an error like the line that continues it, and no NOTE about a quoted string. With the program of 2.2.0 the same failing run had written NOTE: The quoted string currently being processed has become more than 262 bytes long five lines above its ERROR line. The Prompt Builder launches the job through the Job Execution REST API with _contextName set to the context from step 1, and passes everything else (prompt, target LLM, dataset source, metric, optimizer) as job parameters. No secrets travel in the request. Next to the job program ships Create-Optimization-Dataset.sas — a template, not a job: prompt engineers run it (e.g. in SAS Studio) to build a governed CAS dataset table (one column per prompt variable plus a response column) they can pick as the dataset source in the Optimize panel instead of the prompt's own experiments. The panel validates the table's columns and row count before launching; the compute context from step 1 must be able to reach the caslib.

Hosted models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, …) need their provider API key at call time. Both the browser and the job resolve them from the credential domain (default agentic-ai-keys) under the identity of the user who launched the run — set it up once as described in Managing Credentials. Who holds a credential in the domain is the access control for who can spend on optimization; the keys stay out of every request, log, tracker and produced prompt. Self-hosted models without an API_KEY option need no credential.
documents.s: 3. Provide the provider keys via the credential domain

documents.t: In the Visual Analytics report, select the Prompt Builder object and open its Options pane: Option Value Enable prompt optimization (DSPy) Ticked — it is a checkbox. Ticking it reveals the three Optimization: options directly below it and the in-app Optimize step Optimization: compute context The compute context from step 1 Optimization: job path The job's Content path from step 2, e.g. /Public/Jobs/Optimize-Prompt-DSPy Optimization: minimum samples Minimum Best-Response runs required before a run is allowed. Default 30; the panel warns below 50 Credential domain The domain from step 3, among the shared options at the top of the pane. Defaults to agentic-ai-keys; enter none when only key-less models are used (RAG setups cannot be used with none) The three Optimization: options are not shown while the checkbox is not ticked: Visual Analytics reloads the object when the switch changes, and the options appear with the reload. Up to release 2.2 the switch was a dropdown with Enabled and Disabled, and Visual Analytics showed Disabled in it after every reload, whatever was stored. A report saved then keeps its setting: where optimization was enabled, the checkbox is ticked. The compute context set here is the optimization job's only — a deployment that also builds RAG setups sets the ingestion context separately, as RAG: ingestion compute context (see Deploying the Builder UIs). The same values can be supplied as URL parameters (enableOptimization=true&computeContext=...&optimizeJobProgram=...) when the Builder is used outside Visual Analytics. The switch reads true (what Visual Analytics writes for a ticked checkbox), 1, yes or on as enabled; a missing or unreadable value leaves it off.

Everything stays on the prompt-test itself, next to its Prompt-Experiment-Tracker.json — a run creates no additional Model Manager models: An entry in the prompt's Prompt-Optimization-Tracker.json (written only by the job) holding the complete run: dataset/optimizer/metric configuration, metric before/after, the baseline and the optimised prompt, the selected few-shot demos, per-validation-example before/after evaluations, and — for failed runs — the error message the Builder displays. A dataset snapshot (Prompt-Optimization-Dataset-<n>.json), so every optimised prompt stays traceable to the exact examples it was optimised on. The Builder renders these entries as the Optimization history in the Optimize section, where a run can be inspected (evolution details) and loaded back into the workbench as an experiment.

Symptom Cause / fix Job fails immediately: "The optimization job runs as …, not as …, who started it: the compute context … does not run as the user who starts the job" The context runs its sessions under a service account — see step 1. Point Optimization: compute context at a context that runs as the requesting user, such as SAS Studio compute context. Granting the credential to the service account does not help: the write of the result to the prompt is refused. Job fails immediately: "may not write to the prompt … in SAS Model Manager" or "may not remove files from the prompt …" SAS Model Manager refused the user to add a file to the prompt-test or to remove one (the HTTP status is in the message). The result of a run is written there — the user needs the permission to change the prompt-test's project. Job fails immediately: "lacks the dspy package" The compute context's Python is missing the requirements — see step 1. Job fails immediately: "dspy X is too old" The context's dspy predates 3.2.1, which the job's adapter is validated against — upgrade it (pip install -U "dspy>=3.2.1"). Job fails: "MIPROv2 … needs the optuna package" dspy's MIPROv2 requires the optional optuna package — install it in the context's Python (see step 1) or use the bootstrap optimizer. Job fails: "needs an API key for provider …" The credential domain has no entry for that provider for the launching user or their groups — see step 3 and Managing Credentials. A message with "was answered with HTTP …" A request to SAS Viya or to a model container was refused. The message names the status, its name and the message of the answer, for example HTTP 403 (Forbidden). Up to release 2.2 it held the answer as it came, a JSON error whose quotation marks the log shows as backticks. A model container whose score code raised answers HTTP 422 with the line of the raise in its errorMessage: the message gives the text of that raise - HTTP 422 (Unprocessable Entity): No API key: pass the provider key in the API_KEY option of the call. - and the transaction id under which the container logged the traceback. The text is cut at 300 characters, and anything that looks like a key or a token is masked. Launch blocked: "The CAS table … was not found" / "lacks required columns" The dataset table isn't loaded/promoted in that caslib, or its columns don't match the prompt's variables + response — rebuild it with Create-Optimization-Dataset.sas. The flow has no Optimize step Enable prompt optimization (DSPy) is not ticked in the Options pane — the default, and what a report import without saved options leaves behind. For a decision template the step is Evaluate by design. Optimize button disabled: "not fully configured" Optimization: compute context (computeContext) or Optimization: job path (optimizeJobProgram) is blank in the Options pane. Optimize button disabled: "At least N runs …" The prompt has fewer Best-Response runs than the minimum — run and mark more experiments. Launch fails: "is not a Job Execution job definition" optimizeJobProgram doesn't point at the imported job's Content path — see step 2. SCR smoke test fails The SCR endpoint/deployment type in the Options pane is wrong, the target container isn't running, or the key is invalid.

The Administration Guide of the SAS Agentic AI Accelerator will walk you through the setup of this project. Setting everything up will require you to have the following permissions or someone that does: Your user must be part of the SAS Administrators group. You have to have the right to do changes to the kubernetes cluster. You need the ability to setup a Docker compliant container registry. SAS Viya 2026.09 or later. The reports of the transfer package are saved by SAS Visual Analytics of that release (report format BIRD 4.68), which an earlier release may not open, and every measurement in this guide was taken on it.

Please follow these steps, step by step - in order to complete this setup you need both the ability to create a new Repository in the SAS Model Manager (this requires SAS Administrators rights by default), be able to modify the SAS Viya deployment, be able to access a Container Registry and be able to deploy containers in Kubernetes - usually this setup requires both a SAS administrator and a Kubernetes administrator. In order to be able to run this you will need access to a machine with the following tools available: Python 3.11 or newer, for the mdb command line (the Model Definition Builder) that registers and publishes the models kubectl SAS Viya CLI with the authorization, identities, models and transfer plugins installed As a first step clone this repository to the machine and change into the directory: # Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/sassoftware/sas-agentic-ai-accelerator.git # Change into the directory cd sas-agentic-ai-accelerator

# [Optional] Create a new Python environment python -m venv .venv # [Optional] Showcasing the activation on Windows; on Linux/macOS: source .venv/bin/activate .venv/Scripts/activate # Install the mdb command line with the Viya extra (sasctl) - keep the quotes pip install -e "Model-Definition-Builder/cli[viya]" mdb --help Then copy .env.example to .env and fill in the SAS Viya connection - see Setup SAS Model Manager.

Download the SAS Viya CLI from the SAS Support page for your operating system - https://support.sas.com/downloads/package.htm?pid=2512. Here is a link to the SAS Documentation for the CLI. Next we need to setup up a connection profile in order to be able to connect with your SAS Viya environment: sas-viya profile init # Enter your SAS Viya host (service endpoint), select the output type (I recommend fulljson) and enable ANSI colored output (I recommend yes) # If successful you should see a line like: Saved 'Default' profile to /path/.sas/config.json # Next we need to login just to confirm the connection sas-viya auth loginCode # If successful you should see a line like: Login succeeded. Token saved. Next we need to install a couple of plugins (authorization, identities, models & transfer) in order to set everything up correctly - if you want to learn more about the different plugins see the SAS Documentation: # Installing the required plugins - even if you have setup the CLI before I recommend you do this to ensure the plugins are up to date # First up is the authorization plugin sas-viya plugins install -repo SAS authorization # Next we install the identities plugin sas-viya plugins install -repo SAS identities # Then the models plugin sas-viya plugins install -repo SAS models # Finally the transfer plugin - used to import content packages such as the optional Prompt Builder (see "Deploying the Builder UIs") sas-viya plugins install -repo SAS transfer Now the CLI is ready and setup for you to continue on.

This documentation page contains information about the folder LLM-Definitions, which in turn contains information on how to add LLMs to the repository in the SAS Model Manager. Each model is packaged so that it can be deployed using the SAS Container Runtime (SCR). More on the SCR in the SAS Documentation. Each subfolder there contains the definition for one specific LLM - the name of the folder is the model id. A folder is generated from its definition.yaml by the Model Definition Builder (mdb add, mdb generate); the files inside - the score script, inputVar.json/outputVar.json, modelConfiguration.json, options.json, requirements.json, README.md, Model-Card.md - are derived from it and should not be edited by hand. The _Base_Definition folder is a reference copy of that file set from before mdb, kept for orientation.

Tags are being used to provide additional information and filtering options around the LLMs inside of SAS Model Manager. Below you'll find a table with short description and its impact (if any): Tag Description Impact Open-Source Indicates that the model has an open-source license - Proprietary Indicates that the model is proprietary - deprecated Indicates that the models is no longer supported The model will not show up in the Prompt Builder UI small Indicates the required resources for serving this model is small Can be used for when publishing to SCR as a sizing indication medium Indicates the required resources for serving this model is medium Can be used for when publishing to SCR as a sizing indication large Indicates the required resources for serving this model is large Can be used for when publishing to SCR as a sizing indication LLM Indicates that the model has more than 7 billion parameters - SLM Indicates that the model has less than or equal to 7 billion parameters - There is a lot more tags available like MIT-License, Apache-2, Google, etc. these are used to showcase the specific model license and the model provider but have no further impact and new once are added as the market evolves.

Here is a list of models in this repository that are gated on Hugging Face and thus require you to first accept a license - this is sometimes also related to a waiting time until you are confirmed for access. These three still download their weights during the container build (their requirements.json is hand-maintained); the supported way to serve a gated model is to stage the weights on the shared volume instead - see Serving Open-Weight Models. Llama 3.3 70B is served through OpenRouter and needs no Hugging Face access. Model Name Model Provider Hugging Face Link Note Llama 3.2 1B Meta https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct Llama 3.2 3B Meta https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct Mistral Nemo Mistral https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Nemo-Instruct-2407 While it runs on just CPU a hosting provider is recommended.
