documents.t: The logs from the LLM containers is standardized across all of the different models. This has been done in order to be able to parse all of the relevant information from the logs and create monitoring on top of them. In order to make use of these logs, which are written to the standard out of each container, you must collect the logs. If you do not have an established logging and monitoring process, you can use the simplified logging script provided below. Otherwise, if you do have an established way of collecting logs, ensure that you can export them to a folder that can be accessed from SAS Studio as a .log file (as that it is the input for the parsing utilities). The file has to hold the lines as the containers wrote them: the parser only reads a line that starts with <timestamp> - <logger> - <level> - , so a timestamp, a pod name or a JSON wrapper that your process adds to each line has to be removed again. If it is not, the parser reads no request and says so with a warning in the SAS log. The lines of each container also have to stay together in the file, as kubectl logs writes them: an export that orders the lines of all containers by their time is read with gaps, see Requests that run at the same time. For more information on how to parse the log and load it into SAS please take a look at SAS-Viya-Integrations/Logging-Monitoring. Three programs of that folder work on the collected log, and they run in this order: Collect the log - the script below, or your own process. Parse it: Log-Parser-Code.sas or the LLM - Log Parser custom step write one row per request to the table LLM_LOGS - see Running the Parser and The Columns of LLM_LOGS. Pull what the Prompt Builder keeps in SAS Model Manager: Get-All-Prompts.sas or the LLM - Get All Prompts custom step write the experiments, the RAG setups and a catalog of models - see The Experiments of Every Kind. Link the two: Link-Logs-To-Models.sas fills, for every row of LLM_LOGS, the SAS Model Manager id of the model that answered and of the prompt, decision template or RAG setup that sent the request - see Linking the Log to the Models. Steps 2 to 4 of release 2.3.0 ran as one chain on the test system three times, on 2026-10-11 and twice on 2026-10-12, each time with the programs as they were then - the parse with its 24 further columns, the pull with its four further tables, the link, and the joins of the tables: see The Chain on SAS Viya. The first run found defects and the three programs were changed; the second run measured those changes and found further defects, and the programs were changed again; the third run measured those changes - version 2.4 of the LLM - Log Parser step, version 2.2 of the LLM - Get All Prompts step, Link-Logs-To-Models.sas and the ingestion job of a RAG setup. Of what was changed after the third run, the settings a program takes only where they are not set (Settings that stay yours), Load-Fact-Sheets.sas through the job Load-Accelerator-Tables, and Build-RAG-Cost-View.sas with one and with two run tables were measured later that day in test content roots. On 2026-10-13 the collection script as it was that day - with its line in front of the lines of every container, without escape_llm_log - collected the model pods of the test system, and the three code files of that day parsed, pulled and linked that file in a test content root; Build-RAG-Cost-View.sas as it is since it leaves at the first refusal ran there as well: see The Pass of 2026-10-13. Later that day the collection script with escape_llm_log collected the pods again, and version 2.7 of the parser as a code file, the pull and the link ran on that file: see The Second Pass of 2026-10-13. Not run in SAS, and the sections say which part that is: the two steps as steps in any version after 2.4 and 2.2 - the two passes of 2026-10-13 ran the code files -, the rules of version 2.7 for which the collected file holds no case, the collection script with sed in the C locale, and the counter of an optimizationId. The Python of the three programs runs in the tests of the repository and was run outside of SAS on the collected log of those runs. What Was Measured is about the parser as it was before the further columns. What the containers log The shipped deployment templates set SAS_SCR_LOG_LEVEL_SCR_IO=TRACE, and the parser depends on it: the Request: POST / Request Data: lines carry the inputs and the options of every call, and the lines of the score code the token counts, the run time and the answer. For an LLM that is the system prompt, the user prompt and the full response; for a decision model the state, the questions and every answer with its confidence; for an embedding model the embedded text. That is what makes the usage report possible, and it also means prompt text and responses land in your log pipeline. Of an embedding call the table keeps the hash of the text in place of the text, and it also keeps the options of every call without their keys and the first error of a request that failed. Decide who may read the collected log file and the LLM_LOGS table accordingly, or lower the level and forgo the report. The containers also log secrets At this level a container writes more than prompts. The options of a request are logged as they arrive, and for every model that is called with a provider key they hold it as API_KEY:<the key>. The request headers are logged too, and a call from the browser (the Prompt Builder) carries the user's Cookie header. Both must not reach a file that SAS Studio users can open: the collection script below replaces them with REDACTED before a line is written, and an established logging process needs the same step. The redact_llm_log function of the script expects the lines as the container wrote them, which is how kubectl logs prints them without --timestamps or --prefix: its three header expressions match a header at the start of a line, and only the API_KEY expression finds its text anywhere in a line. A process that puts a timestamp or a pod name in front of every line, or wraps the line (the log files of the container runtime, JSON), has to redact before that happens or adapt the three header expressions. The redaction only covers the files and tables the accelerator writes: kubectl logs and a cluster log pipeline still read the key and the cookie. A model whose key the container holds (mdb add --auth env) is called without API_KEY, so its key does not reach the log unless a caller still sends one; its route then has no authentication of its own and needs an allowlist or a NetworkPolicy (Container Deployment). A log file collected without this redaction - with the script of release 2.2.0 or earlier, for example - may contain provider keys and session cookies. Delete those files, including copies and backups, and rotate every provider key that was in use while they were collected. The LLM_LOGS table never held either and does not need to be rebuilt for this: the parser never copied the key or a header into it. The parser of this release keeps the options of a request and replaces the keys in them itself, and of the headers it keeps the X-Request-Id and the kind of client.

Only use this script if you do not have a more robust process in place. Create a script—for example collect_llm_logs.sh—and ensure that it is executable. Use the code below and change both the namespace and the log path. The namespace should be the namespace into which you have deployed the models, and the path needs to be reachable from inside of SAS Studio. The path below is an example and site specific - see Getting the File to the SAS Compute Server for what it assumes and for a way without it. You can also change the logging interval; note that any changes you make here will have to be reflected in the entry for the crontab. The default here also replaces the log file, as the assumption is that you pick up the new entries using the parsing script and append them to the table (a full replacement is also supported). The parser appends only where it is told to: set %let _log_append_table = 1; in front of it, see Appending. With %let _log_append_table = 0; it replaces the table by the requests of the one file, and without the setting it stops at a table that holds rows. # Set the script variables for your environment llm_namespace="llm" llm_log_path="/viya-share/pvs/sasdata/data/llm/llms.log" llm_logging_interval="1h" # Selects the model pods: the deployment templates label each of them app=<model name> llm_pod_selector="app" # Replaces the secrets in the container log with REDACTED: the provider key in the # options of a request and the values of the Cookie, Authorization and X-CSRF-TOKEN # request headers (in any spelling of upper and lower case, which needs GNU sed). # sed runs in the C locale, where every byte is a character: in a UTF-8 locale a byte # that is no UTF-8 ends a match, and what stands behind it would stay as it is redact_llm_log() { LC_ALL=C sed -E \ -e "s/(API_KEY:)[^,}'\"]*/\1REDACTED/g" \ -e 's/^((.* Request Headers: )?Cookie:).*/\1 REDACTED/I' \ -e 's/^((.* Request Headers: )?Authorization:).*/\1 REDACTED/I' \ -e 's/^((.* Request Headers: )?X-CSRF-TOKEN:).*/\1 REDACTED/I' } # Keeps the lines of a container apart from the line this script writes in front of them: a # line of a container that starts like that line - at its start or behind a carriage return, # with or without backslashes in front - gets one more backslash in front, which the parser # takes off again. The last line of a container is ended where it is not (needs GNU sed) escape_llm_log() { sed -E \ -e 's/(^|\r)(\\*#=# llm-log-collection )/\1\\\2/g' \ -e '$a\' } # The time of this collection, in UTC: the same in the line in front of every container llm_collected_at="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" # Remove the next line to append to the log file instead rm -f "$llm_log_path" for pod in $(kubectl get pods -n "$llm_namespace" -l "$llm_pod_selector" -o name); do for container in $(kubectl get -n "$llm_namespace" "$pod" -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'); do # One line in front of the lines of each container: the parser ends a part of the file there { printf '#=# llm-log-collection pod=%s container=%s collected=%s #=#\n' "${pod#pod/}" "$container" "$llm_collected_at" kubectl logs -n "$llm_namespace" "$pod" -c "$container" --since="$llm_logging_interval" | escape_llm_log } | redact_llm_log >> "$llm_log_path" done done The script reads the model pods only. -l app selects every pod that carries a label named app, which the shipped deployment templates set to the name of the model. The pod of a stage-weights job does not carry it and stays out of the file, and so does every other workload that is labelled differently. If something else in your namespace is labelled app as well, give the model deployments a label of their own and set llm_pod_selector to it (for example llm_pod_selector="accelerator=model"). The script reads every container of every model pod on its own, and writes one line in front of its lines: #=# llm-log-collection pod=<pod> container=<container> collected=<time of the collection, UTC> #=#. All lines of one run carry the same time. A container can write a line of that shape - a model writes what it is asked for, and its response is logged line by line -, so the script keeps the two apart: escape_llm_log puts a backslash in front of every line of a container that starts like the line of the script, at the start of a line and behind a carriage return, with or without backslashes in front, and it ends the last line of a container where kubectl logs did not. In a file this script wrote, a line of that shape is therefore a line of the script. The redaction leaves the line of the script as it is and makes no other line a line of that shape. The parser ends a part of the file at each such line and nowhere else, whatever time of collection the line carries, and takes the backslash off again, so a response holds the line as the model wrote it: a request that was running when its container was collected ends there without a response and without an error - failed is missing, and a NOTE counts it - and no line of one container is taken for a line of another. A file without such lines - collected with the script of release 2.2.0 or earlier, or by a process of your own - is read by the time of its lines, as before, and so is what stands in front of the first such line in a file that is appended to across the upgrade. In those lines nothing was put in front of a look-alike: a line of that shape in a response there is read as the line of the script. It ends the response, its request has no status and failed is missing - the NOTE counts it -, and the lines behind it are read as one part up to the next line of the shape. No code can tell it from the line of the script: a file with such a line in a response and a file in which the first collection of this release begins in the middle of that response are the same line for line, and a test of the repository holds the two. So start a new file with the script of this release instead of appending to a file of an earlier one. A process of your own can write the same line in front of the lines of each container it collects; it then has to put the backslash in front as the script does. The pod is no column of LLM_LOGS. On 2026-10-13 the script as it was that day - without escape_llm_log - collected the nine model pods of the test system and wrote nine such lines, all with one time of collection, and Log-Parser-Code.sas of that day read the file (The Pass of 2026-10-13). The script with escape_llm_log, and version 2.7 of the parser, which takes the backslash off, ran in the tests of the repository only - the script with a kubectl of the test that answers from files and with GNU sed 4.9 of Git for Windows, which drops a carriage return in front of a line feed, so the lines that end with both were held by their rows and not by their bytes. They have not run in a live pass and are not run in SAS. The redaction happens in the pipe, so an unredacted line is never written to disk, and the parser reads a redacted log exactly like an unredacted one. redact_llm_log runs sed in the C locale (LC_ALL=C), where every byte is a character. In a UTF-8 locale GNU sed matches a byte that is no UTF-8 with neither . nor a bracket expression, and the function as it was first written for this release - without the locale - redacted the value of a header or of API_KEY only up to such a byte. Measured on 2026-10-13 with GNU sed 4.9 of Git for Windows and the expressions of the script: in the locale en_US.UTF-8 and in C.UTF-8 the line Cookie: abc<FF>secret-value (<FF> being the byte 0xFF) became Cookie: REDACTED<FF>secret-value, and x API_KEY:sk-abc<FF>secret, y became x API_KEY:REDACTED<FF>secret, y; in the C locale they became Cookie: REDACTED and x API_KEY:REDACTED, y. A shell that a cron job starts often runs in the C locale already, an interactive one usually does not. The function with the locale is not run on Linux or against a cluster; the tests of the repository run it with GNU sed 4.9 of Git for Windows. The four sed expressions cover what the containers are known to log; if your requests carry a secret in another header, add a line for it. An hour without a single request leaves a file without requests. The parser reports that with a note and leaves the LLM_LOGS table as it is. Next add the following entry to your crontab (crontab -e), adjusting your path to the script: 0 * * * * /viya-share/pvs/sasdata/data/llm/collect_llm_logs.sh This entry will run the log collection script at the top of every hour.

The paths of this guide are examples, and both are site specific. The script writes to /viya-share/pvs/sasdata/data/llm/llms.log and the parser reads the path that %let _log_path = sasserver:/export/pvs/sasdata/data/llm/llms.log; names where _log_path is not set - the statement a site sets its own path with, in front of the program (Settings that stay yours). The two name the same file only on a system where the host that runs the script and the SAS compute server mount the same storage under these two paths. Set llm_log_path to the file as the collecting host sees it and _log_path to the same file as a compute session sees it, with sasserver: in front: the parser reads the file from the file system of the compute server, stops with an error for any other location and does not read from SAS Content. Whether a compute session sees a directory can be asked in that session, exists=1 means it does: data _null_; exists = fileexist('/export/pvs/sasdata/data/llm'); put exists=; run;
documents.s: Getting the File to the SAS Compute Server

documents.t: On the test system (SAS Viya 2026.09, measured on 2026-10-11) there is no such mount: in a compute session neither /export nor /viya-share existed, and the workstation that collected the logs shares no directory with the compute server. The file went through SAS Content there: The script of this guide wrote the redacted file to a local directory of the collecting host (llm_log_path). The file was uploaded to a folder in SAS Content with the Files service: POST /files/files with the folder as parentFolderUri, the file as the body and its name in the Content-Disposition header. The job that runs the parser first copied the file from SAS Content into the compute session, with a FILESRVC file reference and fcopy, and the parser then read the copy: /* Copy the collected file from SAS Content to the SAS compute server */ filename llmsrc filesrvc folderpath='/Users/<user>/My Folder/<folder>' filename='llms.log' recfm=n lrecl=32767; filename llmdst '/tmp/llms.log' recfm=n lrecl=32767; data _null_; length msg $300; rc = fcopy('llmsrc', 'llmdst'); msg = sysmsg(); put 'Copy of llms.log: ' rc= msg=; run; filename llmsrc clear; filename llmdst clear; /* Set the path in front of Log-Parser-Code.sas: the program takes _log_path where it is set */ %let _log_path = sasserver:/tmp/llms.log; From release 2.3.0 on the last line stands in front of the program - in a program of your own that then includes the shipped file, see Settings that stay yours: Log-Parser-Code.sas takes _log_path only where it is not set. That is how the program ran in The Second Pass of 2026-10-13, with its settings in front of the shipped file. Up to then the program set _log_path itself, in a %let line among its first lines, so a %let that only stood in front of it had no effect and the line of the program had to be changed. Both were measured on 2026-10-11, with the program of that day. With the block in front and the program's own line changed to sasserver:/tmp/llms.log, the parser wrote the 174 rows of the file. With the block in front of the unchanged program, the copy went through and the program then read its default path: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/export/pvs/sasdata/data/llm/llms.log', then ERROR: The log could not be parsed, ..., and the job ended as failed. The custom step has no such line: there the copy is the file the step is given as its log. These are the statements that ran. On 2026-10-11 they ran as they are printed here, with only the folder filled in - one below the My Folder of the user who ran the job: the log said Copy of llms.log: rc=0 msg=, and the copy had the size and the MD5 digest of the uploaded file (558,176 bytes). In the first runs, earlier that day, each collection had a file name of its own; fcopy returned 0 there as well, and a file of 0 bytes arrived as a file of 0 bytes. /tmp is a directory that existed in the compute session of that system - the fileexist step above gave exists=1 for it and exists=0 for /export/pvs/sasdata/data/llm; take one your compute server can write to. The three steps were started one after the other, not from a crontab entry. The file in SAS Content holds the prompts and the responses like the log itself, so whoever may read that folder reads them (see the note at the top of this page).

Log-Parser-Code.sas and the LLM - Log Parser custom step hold the same program. The README of SAS-Viya-Integrations/Logging-Monitoring describes the table it writes, what a row holds for each kind of model and what happens to a table that already exists. The two differ in what they bring along: Log-Parser-Code.sas and the LLM - Log Parser custom step reach a site with the transfer package, in the folder Logging and Monitoring of the content folder (Install or upgrade with the transfer package); from a checkout, mdb content-deploy brings both. A registered step is updated in place - PUT /dataFlows/steps/{id} with the file and its id, answered 200 with the id kept when it was measured on 2026-10-11 and on 2026-10-12 -, which is what mdb content-deploy does: a step that is deleted and uploaded again gets a new id, and saved flows that use it then have to be given the step again. The import and the deploy bring the step to its path of this release, Logging and Monitoring/LLM - Log Parser.step. A step your flows use from another folder - the starter package of earlier releases had it in Custom Steps - is not touched by either: update it in place from a checkout with mdb content-deploy --only "Logging and Monitoring/LLM - Log Parser.step" --to "<path or id of your step>", see One part, somewhere else. Measured on 2026-10-13 in two test content roots: with the path of a registered step of that name the line said equal and named the step and its folder; with the id of a step of another name nothing was written and the line asked for --force, and with --force the step was updated with its id kept. A flow or a job that runs the step more than once in one SAS session needs the step of release 2.3.0. That step announces 36 columns to a flow; a flow that holds an older step announces twelve. A copy of the package SAS Agentic AI Accelerator.json of earlier releases must not be imported for the parser: that starter package holds the step and the code file of May 2025 - twelve columns, LLM calls only, and the session check that fails in a second run. Log-Parser-Code.sas starts a CAS session itself (cas mysess;) when neither the session the SAS option SESSREF names nor a session mysess is connected - a connected mysess is used, and the option is set to it -, assigns the librefs public and casuser and takes each of its settings where the macro variable is not set when it starts (Settings that stay yours). The session and the two librefs stay when the program ends. _log_target_table_lib names a libref: the program looks up the caslib behind it and, when no libref of that name is assigned, hands the value to CAS as the name of the caslib. The custom step is the same program without those first lines, so it takes the following from the SAS session it runs in. Run the chain in a compute context that runs as you The parser and the link program hand their rows to CAS from Python, in the CAS session of the SAS session they run in. In a compute context whose servers run as a service account - on the test system the SAS Job Execution compute context, which runs as sas-be-sa - that fails: Session reconnect failed: Users can only reconnect to their own sessions, then ERROR: The log could not be parsed, the table Public.LLM_LOGS was left as it is., and Get-All-Prompts.sas cannot read SAS Model Manager either. Measured on 2026-10-22; in the SAS Studio compute context, which runs as the user, the same code ran. For a scheduled chain pick such a context (_contextName of the job, or the context of the compute session you submit to).

The five programs of the folder Logging and Monitoring - Log-Parser-Code.sas, Get-All-Prompts.sas, Link-Logs-To-Models.sas, Load-Fact-Sheets.sas and Build-RAG-Cost-View.sas - take a setting only where its macro variable is not set when the program starts. Up to release 2.2 the settings were %let lines at the top of each file, so a newer file, or an import of the content folder, replaced the values of a site with the defaults. Keep your values in a program of your own that sets them and includes the shipped file from the content folder; the shipped file can then be replaced without a value of yours in it: %let _log_path = sasserver:/data/llm/llms.log; filename shipped filesrvc folderPath='/SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/Logging and Monitoring' filename='Log-Parser-Code.sas'; %include shipped; Program Settings, and what the program takes where one is not set Log-Parser-Code.sas _log_path (sasserver:/export/pvs/sasdata/data/llm/llms.log), _log_target_table_engine (CAS), _log_target_table_lib (Public), _log_target_table_name (LLM_LOGS), _log_append_table (no default: 1 appends, 0 replaces, and without a value the program stops at a table that holds rows - see Appending), _log_promote_table (1), _log_save_table (1) Get-All-Prompts.sas The eleven settings under Settings of the pull Link-Logs-To-Models.sas The twelve settings under Settings of the Link Load-Fact-Sheets.sas _lfs_path (/SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/Data), _lfs_caslib (Public) Build-RAG-Cost-View.sas _rcv_fact_caslib (Public), _rcv_runs_caslib (Public), _rcv_runs_tables (RAG_HR_RUNS; several tables separated by commas, with or without blanks around them), _rcv_out_caslib (Public), _rcv_out_table (RAG_RUN_COST) Set means that the macro variable exists. A variable that is set and empty stays empty. For _gap_llm_project, _gap_embedding_project and _gap_decision_project an empty value leaves the models of that kind out of the catalog. Each program deletes its settings at its end, with its other macro variables, as before. A program of yours therefore sets them every time, in front of the include. For the parser that includes _log_append_table: a second include in one SAS session without its %let line is a run without the setting, which stops at a table that holds rows. Measured on 2026-10-13: the first include, with 1, appended; the second, with the log and the table set again and _log_append_table not, wrote its ERROR line and left the 4,654 rows and the saved file as they were. A macro variable of that name that something else left in the SAS session counts as set - a run of the program that was cancelled before its end, for one. Of the parser such a run leaves _log_path without its sasserver:, which the next run refuses. Start a new SAS session, or delete the variable with %symdel. The two custom steps are not affected. A step gets every setting from one of its controls, and the program inside a step has none of these lines. Before the first run on a table of an earlier release - a site that upgrades from 2.2.x and has an LLM_LOGS -, read Appending: the parser of this release stops at that table until _log_append_table is set. The defaults are the values the %let lines had, but for _log_append_table, whose line held 0 and which has no default any more: the other 36 settings of the five programs were compared with them in the code. Measured on the test system on 2026-10-12 with the parser, the pull and the link, each from a program like the one above - the settings, then the include of the shipped file from a test content root: The parser with _log_path, _log_target_table_lib and _log_target_table_name set wrote its table under that name into that CAS library: 1040 rows and 36 columns, promoted and saved, so the four settings that were not set had their defaults. Behind the include none of the seven _log_ variables was left, and Public.LLM_LOGS had the rows and the modified time it had before. The pull with the CAS library and the five table names set wrote its five tables there - 318 rows and 61 columns, 27 and 32, 17 and 26, 107 and 40, 421 and 21 -, the tables of those names in Public were as before, and the eleven _gap_ variables were gone. With %let _gap_decision_project = ; the catalog had 416 rows instead of 421; that the five rows are the decision models was not read. The link wrote 1040 of 1040 rows ... linked against 421 catalog rows, and the twelve _lnk_ variables were gone. Build-RAG-Cost-View.sas ran the same way with one run table, see The Third Run. Load-Fact-Sheets.sas took _lfs_path and _lfs_caslib from the job Load-Accelerator-Tables, which sets both in front of its include (The tables of the reports). Not run: a program with its defaults, which writes Public; and whether the control variables of a step stay behind it in a SAS Studio session, where a code file run next would take them for settings.

A CAS session. The step asks the SESSFOUND function whether the session that the SAS option SESSREF names is connected - that is the session its CAS actions run in. When it is connected, the step starts no session, runs in that one and does not end it. When it is not and a session llmLogMySess is connected, the step sets the option to that session (options sessref=llmLogMySess;), runs in it and does not end it either. Otherwise the step starts a session of its own (cas llmLogMySess;) and ends it as its last action. A table that is not promoted belongs to the session that created it, so of a run with a session of its own only what Promote the table to global scope or Save the table kept is left. The option goes on naming a session that was ended: on the test system _CASNAME_, _SESSREF_ and the option SESSREF still named LLMLOGMYSESS after such a run, while cas _all_ list; listed no session, and SAS wrote NOTE: The default CAS session LLMLOGMYSESS identified by SAS option SESSREF= was terminated. Use the OPTIONS statement to set the SESSREF= option to an active session. That is why the step does not go by a name, and why statements of your own that follow the step in the same SAS session and need CAS have to start a session or set SESSREF to one. The libref of the output table. SAS Studio hands the step the output table as a libref and a table name. The step looks the libref up in dictionary.libnames and writes to the caslib it finds there. When the libref is not assigned in the session, nothing is found and the name of the libref is handed to CAS as the name of the caslib - which is the caslib you chose only where the two have the same name, as with CASUSER and PUBLIC. Without the libref the lines SAS Studio adds behind the step also report the output table as not existing: in the job that had a CAS session and no libref, the log held the line _FLW_ACTION_TABLE_|CASUSER|<table>|0, where the job with the libref had |1. The table was there - promoted, saved and read from a new CAS session with its 174 rows. What SAS Studio does with that line in a flow was not looked at; assign the libref in front of the flow to have it report the table. The caslib CASUSER of the user who runs the step. The parsed rows are uploaded there as _TEMP_LLM_LOGS, and the staging table is dropped at the end. In replace mode they are copied from there to <table>_NEW in the caslib of the output table; in append mode a DATA step reads them from there. Two more tables of the program can stand there for the time of a run: _TEMP_LLM_LOGS_SEEN, the transaction IDs of the table a run appends to, and _TEMP_LLM_LOGS_SAVED, the saved file of a table that is not in memory, loaded to count its rows by a run that replaces and by a run of Log-Parser-Code.sas without the setting. Two librefs and a work table of its own, in append mode. To append to a table that exists, the program assigns _llmtgt to the caslib of the output table and _llmsrc to CASUSER, asks CAS for the columns of the existing table (kept in work._log_target_columns while it is read, then deleted), writes the existing rows and the new ones to _TEMP_LLM_LOGS_ALL in the caslib of the output table with a DATA step, and clears both librefs. The DATA step reads the output table through _llmtgt, so the name of the table has to be one a libref can address (32 characters at most). Log-Parser-Code.sas does the same. The append ran on the test system on 2026-10-11, see Appending. PROC PYTHON with the pandas and swat packages, and what Python needs to reach CAS: the SAS options CASHOST and CASPORT, the certificate file named in the environment variable SSLCALISTLOC and the token in SAS_SERVICES_TOKEN. The Python code connects to the CAS session of the step with them. The code SAS Studio generates for a flow provides neither a CAS session nor the libref: the code generated on the test system for a flow of the step and its output table held no cas and no libname statement. The measurements ran that code unchanged as SAS Job Execution jobs, with the output table in CASUSER, in three kinds of session. The first had these two lines in front (the name of the session is free): cas mysess; libname casuser cas caslib='casuser'; The second had the cas statement alone in front, and the third neither of the two, so that the step started its own session. What Was Measured has what each of them did. These runs were made with the step as it was earlier on 2026-10-11, which started its own session where the macro variable _CASNAME_ did not exist. The step now reaches the same two branches through SESSFOUND, and with that check it was run again later that day: see The Session Check with SESSFOUND.
documents.s: What the Custom Step Takes from the Session

documents.t:
The parser says in the SAS log what it did with the output table: NOTE: The log contains no requests, the table . was left as it is. - an empty log, or one that holds no scoring request. WARNING: Python-Subprocess - No request was read: 'Request: POST' was found in line(s) that do not start as a log line ..., followed by the same note - the lines of the log carry something in front, see the top of this page. ERROR: The log could not be parsed, the table .
was left as it is. - the Python code did not finish, for example because the file is missing. Measured for a file that is missing: the line stood below ERROR: Unhandled Python exception. and a traceback that ends in FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '', SYSCC was 1012 and the job ended as failed. An error that says The saved table .
could not be loaded, nothing was appended and the saved file was left as it is. (append), The saved table .
could not be loaded, nothing was replaced and the saved file was left as it is. (replace: the rows of a table that is only its saved file are counted before anything is written, and where the file can not be loaded nothing is written) or The new table could not be created, the table .
was left as it is. (replace and append). In append mode that line goes on with what the DATA steps returned: The DATA step that appends ended with the return code and wrote rows, the table held and the log , and rows of the table were taken out for

rows of the log (-1 stands for a table that was not found). The DATA steps that leave out the requests the table holds already ended with the return code . Measured on 2026-10-13 with version 2.8, whose line did not name the rows that were taken out, and with a table whose name has 33 characters, which no libref addresses: both return codes 1012, -1 rows written, the table with its 1,024 rows as before, SYSCC 1012 and a failed job. In append mode, a table that the run loaded from its saved file for the append is dropped again behind that line, so only its saved file is left, as before the run; a table that was in memory before the run stays. ERROR: The table .

holds rows and _log_append_table is not set, so nothing was read and nothing was written - not the table and not its saved file. Set it in front of the program: %let _log_append_table = 1; adds the requests of the log to the table, %let _log_append_table = 0; replaces the table with them. - Log-Parser-Code.sas was run without a value of _log_append_table and the table holds rows, in memory or only as its saved file. It is the one line of such a run, written in front of the log. Set 1 or 0; see Appending. The custom step never writes it: its checkbox sets one of the two. ERROR: The rows of the table .
could not be counted and _log_append_table is not set, so nothing was read and nothing was written - not the table and not its saved file. Set it in front of the program: %let _log_append_table = 1; adds the requests of the log to the table, %let _log_append_table = 0; replaces the table with them. - Log-Parser-Code.sas was run without a value of _log_append_table, table.tableExists found the table in memory, and the listing of its rows (table.tableInfo) named no table. It is the one line of such a run, written in front of the log. Set 1 or 0; see Appending. A run with 0 replaces such a table and writes no NOTE of the rows it held. The custom step never writes it. ERROR: CAS refused or did not run an action that the count of the rows of the table .
needs and _log_append_table is not set, so nothing was read and nothing was written - not the table and not its saved file. - Log-Parser-Code.sas ran without a value of _log_append_table, and CAS refused table.tableExists of the table or table.fileInfo, the listing of the saved files of a table that is not in memory; the ERROR lines of CAS stand above it. Nothing was read or written, and the job ends as failed. New in version 2.10 of the step; the words or did not run since version 2.11. ERROR: CAS refused or did not run an action that the run needs for the table .
, nothing was appended and neither the table nor its saved file was written. (append), or the same line with nothing was replaced (replace) - CAS refused one of the actions the run goes by: table.tableExists of the table (in front of the load of its saved file or behind it), table.fileInfo, table.columnInfo of the table, or the listing of CASUSER that counts what is left of the rows of the log; its ERROR lines stand above. The table and its saved file are as before, and a table the run loaded from its saved file for the append is dropped again. Up to version 2.9 of the step a refused table.fileInfo was taken for a library without the saved file, and the run saved a new table over that file. A PROC CAS step of the count or of the output macro that halts - its CAS session ended, say - runs nothing after the action it stopped at. One row per scoring request, whatever kind of model answered it. Column What it holds timestamp, model When the request arrived, and the model it was sent to: the name of its container system_prompt, user_prompt, response For an LLM the two prompts and the response; for a decision model the questions as the JSON that was sent, the state and the answers as JSON; missing for an embedding model temperature, top_p, top_k, max_tokens From the options of the request. max_tokens is read from max_tokens, then max_completion_tokens, then max_length prompt_length, output_length, runtime What the score code logged: input tokens, output tokens, seconds. For an embedding model prompt_length holds its tokens kind llm, embedding or decision, by the names of the inputs of the request (document; questions / state; systemPrompt / userPrompt). Missing when the Request Data: line can not be read status_code The status of the Response: line. Missing when the log holds no such line for the request failed 1 when the log holds an ERROR line for the request, no Response: line although its container went on with another request, or a status of 400 and above; otherwise 0. Missing where the log does not decide it: for a request that was still running where the lines of its container end - at the end of the file or of a part of it -, and for a request that ran at the same time as another one where no line of the log says which of them a response belongs to. See Requests that run at the same time error_text The first ERROR line of the request, cut after 500 characters; for the line the container writes for an exception, with the last line of the traceback added. What has the shape of a key is replaced by REDACTED transaction_id The id the container gave the request (the transaction_<id> logger, the transaction_id of Response Data:) request_id The X-Request-Id header user_agent The kind of client by the User-Agent header: python-requests (the score code of another model, a job, a script), browser, SAS or other. No version, no address and no Referer is kept, and no other header is read embedding_mode The Embedding_Mode option of a call to an embedding model, as sent. Missing when the call sent none; the model then used its default, which the log does not say project The project input of a call to an embedding model (the RAG runtime sends rag) input_hash The SHA-256 of the text an embedding model was given. The text itself is not kept answer, answer_confidence The headline of a decision: the answer to the first question and its confidence. response holds all answers options The options as they were sent, with the value of API_KEY and of every other option that is a secret by its name (key, secret, password, passwd, pwd, credential, authorization, bearer, cookie, a token that is no number) or by its shape (sk-..., Bearer ..., a JWT, 20 and more letters and digits in a row that hold both) replaced by REDACTED. A name also says so with pass or pw as one of its words (my_pass, userPass, pw - not bypass) and with passphrase. Inside a value the user and the password of an address (scheme://user:password@host), a header that carries a secret with everything behind its name, and what follows bearer or basic are replaced as well. The parser does this itself, whether or not the collection redacted the log rag_collection, rag_query_hash For an LLM whose user prompt holds the results of a retrieval: the collection and the SHA-256 of the question. The search tries 500 opening braces of a prompt and decodes 2,000,000 characters at most, so a prompt with more braces than that in front of its retrieval gets no collection model_id, caller_model_id, caller_project_id, caller_kind, caller_name, experiment_run_id, rag_model_id, match_method, match_candidates Written empty by the parser. A request is written once, in every state of the setting. A request is known by three columns together: its transaction_id, its model and its timestamp, the time of its request line. The container writes the transaction ID into the lines of the request, so the three are the same in every file and every run that holds the request; the X-Request-Id header is set outside the container and is not used for it. The ID alone is not taken for the request: the container gives a request its ID unless the client sends one, and a client can send the same ID with every request. Of a request the log itself holds more than once - the lines of a container that were collected twice into one file - one row is written, with 1, with 0 and without the setting: the first that is complete, and the first of all where none is. A row is incomplete when its failed is missing: the lines it was read from hold neither a response nor an error for the request, as for a request that was still running where a collection ended. A run with 1 leaves out a request of the log that the table holds already, with one exception: a complete row of the log takes the place of the rows of the table of its request when each of them is incomplete - a request that was cut off where an earlier collection ended and that a later one holds whole. A complete row of the table is never replaced, and no row is replaced in a table without a numeric column failed. The row that takes the place is the row of the log: what the link wrote into the row it replaces goes with that row, and the link fills the new one at its next run. A table that lacks one of the three columns is compared with nothing. A request without a transaction_id is never taken for another one: it is appended every time it is parsed, and no rule of the program can decide that case - in a file without the lines of the collection script, such a request and another request with the same lines are the same file line for line, and onto a table that holds the row the first has to add nothing and the second a row. In a file of the collection script the line of the script names the pod and the container, but the table keeps neither of a row: the row of such a request of one container and the row of the same request of another container are the same row, so the same file onto the same table has to add nothing in the one case and a row in the other. A column of LLM_LOGS for the pod and the container would tell them apart; the table has none. And a request read again and another request of the same container, written in the same second with the same lines, are the same file line for line with the line of the script as well: no column of the table can tell those two apart. A value that is none. 2, yes, 01 and TRUE each gave the ERROR line of Reading the Job Log and SYSCC 1012; no table was written where there was none, and the copy kept its 3,630 rows and its file. Requests without a transaction ID - a file made by hand, three requests with one and three whose lines name none: the first append wrote 6 rows, a second append of the file added the 3 without an ID again and left out the 3 with one, and a file that held the six twice added 6 and left out 6, 3 in the table and 3 earlier in the log.
