For a definition whose key comes from the container's environment (--auth env) the Deployment reads that variable from a Kubernetes Secret - --key-secret (default llm-api-keys), one entry per variable name - and the command prints how to create it: mdb deploy --all --registry registry.example.com/llm --host viya.example.com \ --tls-secret viya-tls --key-secret llm-api-keys # Create the key Secret once per namespace - ... # kubectl create secret generic llm-api-keys --from-literal=OPENAI_API_KEY="$OPENAI_API_KEY" -n llm # Where the Secret exists already, add or replace these keys - every other key it holds stays: # kubectl patch secret llm-api-keys -n llm --type merge -p '{"stringData":{"OPENAI_API_KEY":"'"$OPENAI_API_KEY"'"}}' The command line holds no key: the shell fills in each value from its own environment (for example after set -a; . ./.env; set +a). To add a key to a Secret that exists, use the kubectl patch line the command prints, not kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -: apply removes every key it applied before that the new manifest does not list, and a mdb deploy <model_id> lists only the variables of that model - the keys of the other models would go, and their pods would fail with CreateContainerConfigError at their next start. The TLS Secret has to exist in the namespace of --namespace (default llm): an Ingress reads no Secret of another namespace, and the command says so when --tls-secret names another one. To serve the models with the certificate of the SAS Viya ingress, copy it into that namespace and renew the copy when the certificate is renewed: # The certificate of the SAS Viya ingress, copied into the namespace of the models (bash) kubectl create secret tls llm-tls-certs -n llm \ --cert=<(kubectl get secret sas-ingress-certificate -n <viya-namespace> -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d) \ --key=<(kubectl get secret sas-ingress-certificate -n <viya-namespace> -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.key}' | base64 -d)

The Python SCR runtime answers only POST /<model_id>. The Ingress of each rendered model rewrites the public path /llm/<model_id>/<model_id> to it with an annotation of the NGINX Ingress controller. Contour, the ingress controller of current SAS Viya deployments, has no rewrite on a plain Ingress, so these Ingresses reach no model there. With --ingress contour the command renders the models without an Ingress and writes one router for all of them, llm-router.yaml, from SCR-LLM-Deployment-YAML/llm-router-contour-template.yaml: mdb deploy --all --ingress contour --registry registry.example.com/llm --host viya.example.com \ --tls-secret llm-tls-certs --dns "$(kubectl get service kube-dns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')" kubectl apply -f deploy-yaml/ # the models' Deployments and Services, and the router curl https://viya.example.com/llm/healthz # ok An Ingress that an earlier mdb deploy without --ingress contour created for a model stays until you delete it (kubectl delete ingress <model-name> -n llm); the command reminds you of it. What the router is. A ConfigMap with an NGINX server block that has one location = /llm/<model_id>/<model_id> per rendered model and forwards it to http://<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:<port>/<model_id>; a Deployment of nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27-alpine (port 8080, readiness on /llm/healthz, requests 20m CPU and 32Mi, limit 128Mi) and its Service; and one Contour Ingress for the path /llm (Prefix) of the host, with the TLS secret of --tls-secret and projectcontour.io/response-timeout: 300s. Contour merges an Ingress for the same host, so the routes of SAS Viya stay as they are. Calls keep their URL: host/llm/model_name/model_name. Render every model at once. The router routes exactly the models of one render. mdb deploy <model_id> --ingress contour warns that applying its llm-router.yaml removes the routes of every other model: render with --all whenever a model is added. The Deployment of the router carries the list of routed models as an annotation, so a changed list restarts it - NGINX reads its configuration only at start. The resolver. NGINX looks each Service up per request through the cluster DNS (resolver <dns> valid=30s ipv6=off), so the router starts before the models and follows a Service that is created again. --dns gives the address of the cluster DNS; the default 10.0.0.10 is that of kube-dns on AKS, and a render without --dns prints it with the kubectl line that reads the address of your cluster. A wrong address fails no apply: the router starts, and every request answers 502. Other limits of the server block: request bodies up to 64 MB and 300-second timeouts. Placing the pods. --node <name> pins the models and the router to one node (nodeSelector on kubernetes.io/hostname); the app=llm node affinity of the templates still applies unless --node-class is given. --node-class <class> replaces that affinity and its tolerations with one toleration of the SAS node taint workload.sas.com/class=<class>:NoSchedule, so the models can run on a node pool of SAS Viya. --requests CPU,MEMORY (default 1000m,4000Mi), --limit-memory and --pull-policy (Always, IfNotPresent or Never) change the model container only; the router keeps its own small requests. These options work with --ingress nginx as well. A value the command cannot use ends it with exit code 2 before anything is written. Small requests are for API wrappers. --requests and --limit-memory apply to every model of the render. Values such as 100m,384Mi with a 1Gi limit suit the models that only call a provider's API; a model that runs its own weights in the container - the hf_transformers LLMs (Qwen, SmolLM), the emb_sentence_transformers embedding models and von_1_2 - needs the defaults or more, and with a 1Gi limit it is ended for lack of memory. Because the router routes exactly the models of one render, render twice and keep the router of the --all run: mdb deploy --all --ingress contour ... --requests 100m,384Mi --limit-memory 1Gi # deploy-yaml/, with llm-router.yaml mdb deploy von_1_2 qwen_25_7b bge_large_en_v15 ... --ingress contour ... --out deploy-self-hosted # the default requests cp deploy-self-hosted/deploy-*.yaml deploy-yaml/ # the Deployments only - not that run's llm-router.yaml, which routes only those models kubectl apply -f deploy-yaml/ Measured on 2026-10-19 without a cluster: the --all run wrote 57 Deployments with the small values and a router with 57 routes; the second run, for the 14 self-hosted definitions, wrote them with 1000m and 4000Mi and no limit, and a router with 14 routes, with the warning that applying it removes every other route. The Deployments of the two runs differ only in resources. No authentication. Like the Ingress of each model, the router answers anyone who can reach host/llm/; restrict who can reach the path as described under --auth env. Without --ingress contour the rendered files are those of earlier releases, byte for byte. The output of --ingress contour was compared with kubectl diff against a cluster that ran a hand-made router of the same design (SAS Viya Stable 2026.09 on AKS, 2026-10-19), without applying it: the router was identical; the model Deployments differed in a label, in SAS_SCR_LOG_LEVEL_SCR_IO (TRACE from the templates, INFO on that cluster - see Container Deployment) and in a readiness probe on /internal/ready (port 8080) that the hand-made Deployments had and the templates do not. Applying the rendered files there would restart each model pod once. Model-Definition-Builder/ci-recipes/ contains thin GitHub Actions pipelines (a workflow_dispatch model-lifecycle job and a weekly deprecation radar) where every step is just an mdb verb.

mdb radar --all checks every managed model against its provider's live catalog; --probe sends one 1-token call per model for ground truth (catalog listing is not an availability guarantee — retired models can stay listed). mdb retire <model_id> tags a definition deprecated (hiding it from the Prompt Builder) and regenerates it. Where it cannot reach SAS Viya to retire the registered model, it says why - The registered model's status was not updated: <the reason> - and keeps the definition tagged.

definition.yaml inside the model folder is the only file you edit. After changing it: mdb generate <model_id> # re-render the generated files mdb sync <model_id> # update the fact-sheet row mdb validate <model_id> # cross-file coherence rules with fix-it hints The *_fact_sheet.csv files (LLM-Definitions/llm_fact_sheet.csv, Embedding-Definitions/embedding_fact_sheet.csv) are a generated artifact — you never edit them by hand. mdb sync <model_id> refreshes a single row; mdb sync --rebuild regenerates each sheet in full from every managed definition (sorted by model_id), creating the file if it does not exist yet: mdb sync --rebuild # rebuild both sheets from the definitions mdb sync --rebuild --prune # also drop rows for models with no definition folder Rebuilding is idempotent (an unchanged fleet produces a byte-identical sheet) and preserves any hand-maintained rows that have no definition folder unless you pass --prune. This is the quickest way to bring the fact sheets in line after a bulk migration instead of syncing each model one by one. RAG ingestion does not read the sheets: rag_core holds a copy of two of their columns, the credential-domain entry of each hosted model (rag_core/providers.py) and the prices of the cost line of the run log (rag_core/pricing.py). After a definition is added, its auth mode switched or a price changed, regenerate both from the sheets and replace the maps in the modules. Until then a new hosted model is sent no key - an enrichment with it stops before the first call and names rag_core/providers.py, an embedding model fails at its first call - and the run log says cost unknown for it: cd SAS-Viya-Integrations/RAG python -m rag_core.providers --from ../../Embedding-Definitions/embedding_fact_sheet.csv python -m rag_core.providers --llm-from ../../LLM-Definitions/llm_fact_sheet.csv python -m rag_core.pricing --from ../../Embedding-Definitions/embedding_fact_sheet.csv python -m rag_core.pricing --llm-from ../../LLM-Definitions/llm_fact_sheet.csv The RAG test suite (SAS-Viya-Integrations/RAG/tests) fails while a map differs from its sheet. To make the sheets available to the SAS Visual Analytics monitoring report, mdb load-facts uploads them to CAS — the Python equivalent of Load-Fact-Sheets.sas. Each sheet is loaded with global scope (promoted, so every session sees it) and saved to the caslib's data source on disk (so it survives a CAS restart), as the tables LLM_FACT_SHEET, EMBEDDING_FACT_SHEET and DECISION_FACT_SHEET. A kind the site has no definition of - no folder in Embedding-Definitions, say - is loaded as an empty table with its sheet's columns, and the command says so in one line: the LLM Usage Report reads the LLM and the embedding table, and the page Start Here looks for all three. A kind that has definitions but no sheet is skipped with the hint to run mdb sync --rebuild first. An existing table of the same name is unloaded first and its saved copy replaced: mdb load-facts # load into the Public library (default) mdb load-facts --caslib MyLib # a different CAS library (env: SAS_CAS_LIBRARY) mdb load-facts --rebuild # regenerate the sheets from the definitions, then load The CAS server defaults to cas-shared-default (auto-detected; override with --server or SAS_CAS_SERVER). This uses the casManagement REST API over the same session the register/publish commands use — no separate CAS connection. The save step writes a .sashdat, so target a path-based caslib (like Public); a database-backed caslib would reject the save.

mdb load-releases turns the repository's CHANGELOG.md into the CAS table ACCELERATOR_RELEASES (same caslib and server options as load-facts; the name comes from --table or SAS_RELEASES_TABLE) and mdb setup loads it by default (--no-releases skips it). It has one row per release - the release intro, change_type = Release - and one per changelog entry, or, for an entry of the Prompt Builder, one per part of the Builder it concerns, with: Column Content version, release_date from the ## [x.y.z] - date heading; an Unreleased section is listed but never current is_current 1 for the newest dated release release_rank, item_rank 1 = newest release; the entry's position within it, so a report can order without dates section, change_type the heading as written and its normalised kind: Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed, Breaking, Upgrade, Release component Prompt Builder, RAG runtime, Credentials, Model Definition Builder, Definitions, Documentation or General - from the section heading when it names one, else from the entry's wording. Entries about the RAG Builder are filed under Prompt Builder, which it is part of, and no entry of a release before 2.0.0 is filed under RAG runtime. An entry whose headline is about the release table itself is filed under Model Definition Builder, and an entry that adds definitions under Definitions when its headline names them and nothing of mdb summary, detail the entry's bold lead (or its first sentence, cut at a word and ended with ... when it is longer than 140 characters) and the rest, as plain text; numbered steps keep their numbers, so that "step 2" can be found builder_part the part of the Prompt Builder an entry concerns: Prompt, Decision or RAG; empty for the release intro and for every component other than Prompt Builder and RAG runtime. The last column It exists because a SAS Visual Analytics Data-Driven Content object needs a data assignment before it renders: the Prompt Builder object is assigned this table, and a report author can filter it by component to show what changed for the Builder next to it. mdb load-releases --csv out.csv writes the table without contacting SAS Viya, for a look at the rows. mdb content-deploy writes the same file into the content folder as Data/ACCELERATOR_RELEASES.csv, and the job Data/Load-Accelerator-Tables of that folder loads it into CAS with the columns and types of this table - for a site that imported the package without mdb, see The tables of the reports. The component is read from the wording with keyword lists, in a fixed order: the first component an entry names is the one it is filed under, the Prompt Builder first. Three things decide before the wording of the entry. A section heading that names a component files every entry under it there - the entries of 2.0.0 under RAG cost are RAG runtime rows, those about the setup editor of the RAG Builder included. And the release: rag_core, the RAG steps and the vector stores came with 2.0.0, so an older entry that "retrieves" or "enriches" something is filed under the next component it names. And a headline about the release table - one that names the release table, ACCELERATOR_RELEASES or mdb load-releases: mdb makes the table, and such an entry names the Prompt Builder, the RAG Builder or the RAG runtime as values of the column, not as what changed, so it is a Model Definition Builder row whatever it names. This holds for the headline only: an entry that names the table in its text, as what a report object is assigned, is filed by its wording (2.0.5 The RAG Builder object in the shipped package has a data assignment is a Prompt Builder row). What the Prompt Builder is recognised by includes its buttons and objects - a prompt-test, the experiment tracker, the judge, the best prompt - and an entry that says it holds for both builders, the Prompt Builder and the RAG Builder of 2.0.0 to 2.2.x. One thing decides after the wording. mdb is the tool and the definitions are what it makes, so an entry that adds definitions says what mdb generated or renders, and its wording files it under Model Definition Builder. It is filed under Definitions when its headline holds the word definitions and nothing mdb is recognised by: 2.2.0 Shipped definitions, and the open-source CPU embedding definitions of 1.1.0. A headline that names the tool as well - mdb sync --rebuild regenerates the fact sheets from the definitions - stays with the tool, and so does one that names a single definition or a definition kind. These two rules were checked on the CSV that mdb load-releases --csv writes from this changelog and by the tests of mdb; they were not run in SAS Viya. The line the command ends with counts the release headings of the changelog, which is not the number of versions: CHANGELOG.md has the heading [0.1.29] twice, for 2025-10-13 and for 2025-10-10. For the changelog of 2.3.0 the command says 58 releases, and the table holds 58 values of release_rank and 57 of version. One row per part of the Builder​ The Prompt Builder holds three parts in one report - prompt templates, decision templates and RAG setups - and builder_part is the column for a button bar that lets a reader of the Changelog page pick one of them. A button bar shows the rows of the value that is picked, so an entry of the component Prompt Builder is written once for each part it concerns: the rows are equal in every column but builder_part, in the order Prompt, Decision, RAG. A row of the component RAG runtime carries RAG, once. Nothing else has a part. release_rank and item_rank are those of the entry on each of its rows, so a change is still counted once by that pair (not by version alone: the changelog used 0.1.29 for two releases); mdb load-releases prints the rows per part beside the number of entries they stand for. Which parts an entry concerns is read from its wording, as the component is. The first of these that applies decides: A section heading that names a part: every entry under it is filed under the parts the heading names, whatever its own headline names. 2.0.0 has the heading RAG Builder: generating what a setup implies, and its entry Deleting a setup says what depends on it first, whose text begins with the Prompt Builder, is RAG alone. The headings Added, Changed, Fixed and Removed name nothing. The steps of an upgrade are written for the whole Builder, and so is an entry that says it holds for all of it: with the words three kinds, every kind, all four create dialogs or both builders. The parts the headline names: a prompt, the judge, the optimization or the Call LLM node for Prompt; a decision template, the decision mode or a decision model for Decision; the RAG Builder, a RAG setup, retrieval, ingestion, the ledger or a vector store for RAG. A prompt-test and an experiment belong to the flow both kinds of template share, so they name Prompt and Decision, and so does a template named without its kind: a prompt, a template or a RAG setup names all three parts. A decision in SAS Intelligent Decisioning names no part. The headline is read whole - for an entry without a bold lead that is its first sentence, also where the column summary holds only the beginning of it. A headline that names the Prompt Builder and no part of it - The create dialogs of the Prompt Builder show the whole name - concerns the Builder as a whole and is written for all three. When the headline settles nothing, the parts the rest of the entry names decide, and an entry that names none anywhere is written for the whole Builder. A template without its kind names nothing here: in the text of an entry the word is as often the score template of a definition or the file a retrieval model is manifested from. In each of them the release has a say: a part that did not exist yet cannot be concerned. Before 2.2.0 there was no decision mode, so no entry of an older release is filed under Decision, and a template without its kind names nothing there. Before 2.0.0 the Builder was the one for prompts, so an entry that names no part is Prompt alone there, Prompt and RAG from 2.0.0, and all three from 2.2.0 - which is also what the whole Builder in the list above means for a release. Up to 2.2.x the Prompt Builder and the RAG Builder were two applications, and the name Prompt Builder names the prompt part in those releases; from 2.3.0 it is the name of the whole. An entry that names the RAG Builder is filed under RAG in any release - the changelog first names it in 0.1.14. The reading is a set of keyword lists (PART_KEYWORDS and its neighbours in mdb/core/releases.py), not an understanding of the entry, and the headline outweighs the text: an entry whose headline names one part is filed under that part even where its text says that another is affected as well. The one exception is a headline about prompts whose text names decision templates, which is filed under both because the two share a flow. Name every part in the headline of a new entry when it concerns more than one, and put an entry that is not about one part under a heading that names none. These rules were checked on the CSV that mdb load-releases --csv writes from this changelog and by the tests of mdb. The table with builder_part was loaded into CAS on the test system on 2026-10-12, by mdb load-releases and by the job Load-Accelerator-Tables, each under a test name: 707 rows and eleven columns, builder_part empty in 341 rows, Prompt in 134, Decision in 54 and RAG in 178. It was not shown on a report page. The Changelog page of the report​ The page needs two things from the table: the filter on component it has (Prompt Builder; add RAG runtime to it to list the changes to the steps and rag_core under the RAG button as well), and a button bar on builder_part as the control a reader picks the part with. Without the filter on component the rows of the other components, which have no part, are rows of the empty value. With Prompt Builder alone in the filter, the RAG button lacks the RAG runtime rows, and among those are entries about the interface of the RAG Builder: 2.0.0 lists some under its headings RAG cost and Enrichment: making a chunk say where it came from, and those headings file every entry under them as RAG runtime. The entries about the release table itself are Model Definition Builder rows with an empty builder_part: a page filtered on Prompt Builder does not list them, and with Model Definition Builder added to the filter no button of the bar shows them - read from the table as CSV, not measured in SAS Visual Analytics. mdb load-releases changes the table and not the report: the page with the button bar comes with the transfer package a maintainer exports after building it, and until that report is imported a site has the new table under the page it had. On that page a Prompt Builder entry that concerns two or three parts is two or three rows of the table, equal in everything the page shows. What the page as shipped up to now makes of them was read from the package and not measured in SAS Visual Analytics: its list table is an aggregated one (detail="false" in the report content) over Version, Component, Summary and Detail, and an aggregated list table has one line per combination of its columns, so such an entry should still be one line there; its button bar on Change Type and its filter on component are not affected. A list table switched to detail data shows the entry once per part, and anything that counts rows - a Frequency, a key value, a bar chart of changes per release - counts it once per part as well. To count entries instead of rows, count under one button of the bar, or take the distinct count of an item that joins release_rank and item_rank. mdb generate --all --check verifies that every generated file matches its manifest and is intended as a CI gate. Files you edited by hand are never overwritten silently — the command tells you to either fold the change into the manifest, declare the file as hand-maintained under generation.overrides, or pass --force.

Existing hand-written folders keep working unchanged and are never touched. To migrate one onto a manifest: mdb import <model_id> # writes definition.yaml, reports what would change mdb import <model_id> --apply # converges the folder onto the generated files The import reports every intended normalization (canonical options parser, provider usage-based token counting, requirements standardization) so you can review the diff — re-test and re-publish affected models afterwards. The second command converges the folder onto the definition.yaml the first one wrote, with the changes you made to it: a folder whose definition.yaml has no .mdb-lock.json beside it is not converged yet, and mdb import reads that definition.yaml as it is - without --apply it lists again what would change. A folder with both files is managed, and mdb import leaves it (already has a definition.yaml - nothing imported.). mdb import <model_id> --apply on a folder without definition.yaml does both steps at once, and mdb pull <model_id> --import writes the definition.yaml of the folder it pulled as mdb import <model_id> does. Where the import cannot render the files, nothing is written and the line names what to repair: for an option whose name or default breaks the rule of options.json, the options.json of the folder; for an option outside the vocabulary that declares no type, taking it out of options.json or adding it to the vocabulary - to keep it outside the vocabulary, run the import without it and declare it inline (type and description) in the definition.yaml it writes before mdb import <model_id> --apply; for a definition.yaml that is not converged yet, that definition.yaml. mdb pull --import refuses a folder in the same way and ends with exit code 1; the pulled files stay.

--offline (or MDB_OFFLINE=true): no outbound calls; model catalogs come from the bundled snapshots and manual entry HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE are honored for all provider calls --no-verify-ssl / MDB_VERIFY_SSL=false corresponds to the -k option of the existing Python scripts

You can declare options that are not part of the standardized vocabulary — useful for provider-specific parameters. Give them an inline type (and a description) in definition.yaml and they are passed to the provider as-is under their own name. mdb generate and mdb validate warn you (rule V010) about what such an option gives up: UIs show it with its raw name and your description instead of a standardized label, and it gets no cross-provider value translation. That is often perfectly fine — the warning just makes it a conscious choice. To standardize an option instead, add it to definition-core/static/option-vocabulary.json with a label, type and per-family mapping. Custom options with informational: true appear in options.json for documentation but are never sent to the provider. Every option mdb writes into options.json keeps the rule the Prompt Builder reads it by: the name of an option holds no comma and no colon, and neither the default of an option other than API_KEY nor a value of an enum is a text with a comma - the Prompt Builder sends the options of a run as one text, {name:value,name:value}; the name of an option has no blank and no quote at its ends, and a text the run sends - the default of an option other than API_KEY, a value of an enum - is one the score code reads as written: no blank and no quote at its ends, not true or false in any case, and no number ("5", "0.5", "TRUE", " a " and "'a'" are not); a number the run sends is one the score code reads as a number: not one the Prompt Builder writes as 1e-7 or 1e+21 - a number below 0.000001 or from 10^21 on with one significant digit; an enum option has a non-empty list of texts as its values, and its default is one of them; the default of a bool option is true or false; the default of API_KEY is the name of the provider key, a non-empty text; the default of any other option is a text, a number, true or false - not null, a list or an object; type, label and description are texts where given; no option holds NaN or Infinity. The second and the third item follow from the parser mdb generates into the score code (_options_parser.py.j2): it takes the blanks and then the quotes off the ends of a name and of a value, reads true and false in any case as true and false, and reads a value as a number where float() reads one that holds a point or int() one that does not. An informational temperature was read as temperature and replaced the temperature of the model; a default TRUE was read as true and 5 as a number. mdb generate - and add, retire and validate (rule V003) - refuses a manifest that breaks the rule with one line naming the option, and writes nothing. For example: my_model: Option 'mode' is an enum option whose values are null - an enum option needs a non-empty list of texts as its values. or my_model: Option 'stop' has the default " a " - the score code would read it as "a", not as that text. A self-hosted model whose provider.params.base_url is null, a list or an object is refused the same way, for its option base_url. mdb import and mdb pull --import refuse a hand-maintained folder in the same way when the name or the default of one of its options, or the key name of its API_KEY, breaks the rule - an API_KEY whose default is no text or an empty one (0, false, "", null), that has no default or that is no object is refused like one whose default is 5; it was taken as no key, the definition became auth.mode: none, and the regenerated options.json lost the API_KEY the score code still read. A definition.yaml whose option holds a default that is null, a list or an object, or another field the schema of definition.yaml does not take, is refused by that schema before the rule is reached: generate and register print the schema's message on one line, validate reports it under rule V001, and retire ends with a traceback. Nothing is written. mdb register refuses a manifest that breaks the rule the same way, and also refuses an options.json it would upload that breaks the rule (one listed under generation.overrides too), before it writes anything to SAS Model Manager. Each refusal is printed on one line, also where the output goes to a pipe or a file, and so are the warning V010 and the note of mdb generate about an option outside the vocabulary, also for a name that holds a line break. The Prompt Builder leaves an empty option of type string out of a run, and the score code then uses its own default. The rule of mdb and its refusals ran on the workstation only, not against SAS Viya.

Options are defined once in the manifest and flow into the score script defaults, options.json and the fact sheet together. Beyond temperature, top_p, top_k and max_tokens, the typed option vocabulary covers seed, frequency/presence penalties, reasoning_effort for reasoning models (which reject temperature/top_p — the generator handles this), max_completion_tokens and thinking_budget for extended-thinking models. The full vocabulary lives in Model-Definition-Builder/definition-core/static/option-vocabulary.json.

reasoning_effort takes five levels for every model: minimal, low, medium, high, maximum. The vocabulary translates them once per score template: the OpenAI-style templates send minimal to high as they are and maximum as high; the environment-configured Azure template sends minimal as none and maximum as xhigh; and the Anthropic template sends output_config.effort, with minimal and low as low and maximum as max. A model that accepts other words than its template carries its own translation on the option in definition.yaml: options: reasoning_effort: default: medium value_map: minimal: none low: low medium: medium high: high maximum: xhigh The keys must be exactly the five levels and the values the words the provider accepts. A missing or extra key, an empty value, or a value_map on an option its template does not translate - a custom pass-through option or an informational one included - is refused by mdb generate, validate (V003) and register. mdb add writes the map from the catalog's list of the effort words a model accepts - minimal to minimal where the model takes it, else to its lowest word, and maximum to its highest - and only where it differs from the template's: gpt_6_luna sends minimal as none and maximum as xhigh, and gpt_61_sol sends minimal as low (it has no none) and maximum as xhigh. For a model the catalog does not know, write the map by hand and run mdb generate.

Claude 5.5 (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) refuses temperature other than 1, top_p and top_k at any value (even top_p 1), and a thinking budget (thinking {type: enabled}); it thinks adaptively and is steered by output_config.effort. mdb add therefore gives these models reasoning_effort (default medium) and max_tokens (default 4000), and no sampling option; a temperature a caller passes anyway is not sent. The thinking counts against max_tokens: a smaller default can end a call before its answer is written, and the Prompt Builder asks a judge for at least 4000 tokens for the same reason. reasoning_effort and thinking_budget exclude each other - keep thinking_budget for older Claude models. The default medium is the API's own for Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5; Sonnet 5.5 defaults to high at the API, so set default: high in its definition.yaml where you want that.

A hosted-API scorer waits runtime.timeout_s seconds for the provider (default 60), then the call fails in the container. A model that reasons before it answers can take minutes at a high effort, so mdb add gives a reasoning model 300, and so do the shipped definitions with a reasoning_effort option. Change the value in definition.yaml, then mdb generate, mdb register --update and mdb publish: runtime: template: openai_chat requirements_profile: api-wrapper timeout_s: 300 Keep it below the time the caller waits: a manifested prompt waits LLMCONTAINERTIMEOUT seconds (600 by default), and the Ingress of the rendered YAML lets a request take 300 seconds (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout, and the router of --ingress contour the same). A self-hosted scorer has no such timeout.
documents.s: How long a call may take

documents.t: The accelerator ingests a document corpus into a vector store and serves it back to a decision. This page is the operations view: what to deploy, what the environment must provide, which knobs matter, and what the product does with your data. For building a pipeline, see the RAG user guide.

Everything lives in one governed SAS Content folder, by default /SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/RAG: Folder Contents rag_core/ The Python runtime every step and job imports at run time steps/ The nine custom steps, registered as dataFlows resources jobs/ Ingest-Documents.sas, the standalone schedulable job, and Test-Retrieval.sas, the probe behind the Builder's Test retrieval models/ The retrieval model template, manifested per setup generated/ Default destination for per-setup artifacts — the ingestion job and the Studio flow the Builder generates, and what RAG - Register Setup writes. The Builder lets an author choose a different folder per setup This is the RAG runtime. It holds no user interface: the RAG Builder that writes setups against it is part of the Prompt Builder — see Serving the RAG Builder below. Two ways put the runtime there: The transfer package. mdb builders-import imports the content folder, and the runtime is the folder RAG of it — see Install or upgrade with the transfer package. The package is compared with the repository before it ships, file by file and step by step, so a site that imports the package of a release has the runtime the documentation and the changelog of that release describe, and needs no script. From a checkout. The shipped script publishes the runtime of your checkout — for a fix between two packages, or for a site that does not import the package: ./SAS-Viya-Integrations/Other/deploy-rag-content.ps1 ./SAS-Viya-Integrations/Other/deploy-rag-content.sh The script calls mdb content-deploy --only RAG --to <the RAG content root> (see One part, somewhere else). It needs the Model Definition Builder installed and a sign-in it can use — a token, a password grant or the login of the SAS Viya CLI. The folder it deploys into is /SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/RAG; -ContentRoot (PowerShell) or -r (bash) names another one: the RAG content root itself, a folder of any name, which is what the option RAG: content root of the Prompt Builder holds. A site with such a content root deploys the runtime there after an import, because the import brings it into the folder RAG of the content folder. -DryRun / -n lists what would change and writes nothing. A folder that is not there is created only with -Create / -c (with every folder above it), so a mistyped path does not become a new folder. A warning mdb writes to the error stream - InsecureRequestWarning where TLS verification is off - does not stop the PowerShell script, also with its streams redirected, and both scripts end with the exit code of mdb. The command they call, mdb content-deploy --only RAG --to <folder>, created the 41 entries of the runtime directly in a test folder on SAS Viya 2026.09 on 2026-10-12. On 2026-10-13 the PowerShell script ran as a dry run for a test folder, with every stream redirected into a file and its command line saved beside it: the file held the warning and 41 entries: 41 equal., and the request log GET requests only; the exit code of the script was not saved. Not run against SAS Viya: the bash script, a run without -DryRun / -n, and -Create / -c. Nothing is ever fetched from the internet at run time, so both ways work in an air-gapped deployment: the SAS Content folder is the distribution channel, not GitHub. If a deploy ends with a line that says FAILED, read the line Stopped at the first write that failed: ... under it and run the deploy again: it stops at the first write that is refused or gets no answer, lists what it did not attempt, and removes nothing, so the folder holds the file it had or the new one. Up to release 2.2 a file was replaced by deleting it and uploading the new copy. Measured on 2026-10-11 on SAS Viya 2026.09 with deploy-rag-content.ps1 as it was then — a script that uploaded the files itself —, against a content folder that held the runtime of release 2.0: the first run stopped after four files with (409) Conflict on the upload of a file (POST /files/files) whose old copy it had just deleted, and left that file missing. The same upload was answered 201 a minute later, and a second run of the script completed with Deployed 35 files. All nine steps had kept their ids, and every file equalled the checkout afterwards. A third run later the same day went through at the first attempt. mdb content-deploy deletes no file: it replaces the content of a file that differs in place, under the id the file has. That update has not run against SAS Viya. Why a deploy and not a manual upload A .step file uploaded as a plain Content file renders as an empty step editor — steps are dataFlows service resources. The deploy also updates an already-registered step in place rather than replacing it. Re-registering a step mints a new id, and every saved flow referencing the old id breaks.

A new runtime in the folder does not reach what a site made from the earlier one. After the package of a new release was imported, or its runtime deployed from a checkout: Open every RAG setup in the Prompt Builder and click Manifest setup. A retrieval model holds the score code it was manifested with, and the job definition of a setup holds a copy of Ingest-Documents.sas from the day it was manifested; the manifest writes the template and the program of the release into them. For release 2.3.0 that is what brings the endpoint a setup embeds at (Where a setup embeds), the TLS setting of the report, the lengths of the variables (The lengths of the variables), the saved ledger that is loaded back (A saved ledger is loaded back), the run lock that follows the column types of the ledger, and a failed run that ends as a failed job. Run the ingestion of each setup once. From release 2.3.0 on the job publishes <prefix>_RUNS and <prefix>_DOC_EVENTS beside the ledger, and that one run publishes every run the vector store holds for the collection (Run history). A job definition that was not manifested again holds the program of the day it was made and publishes neither table. Publish the decisions that use the retrieval model again, so that the destinations run the new score code. No published decision has to be repaired for the lengths of the variables. A setup that was registered from a flow gets the new score code when the step RAG - Register Setup runs again (the checkbox of the step). A job that the step generated from a flow is not written by Manifest setup: run the step again with the flow named under Studio Flow to generate the scheduled job from. A job that SAS Studio itself deploys from the flow does not have the statements that report a failed run as failed. A schedule, a monitor or a script that reads the state of the ingestion job has to expect a new state from release 2.3.0 on: a run that failed ends as failed. Up to 2.2.x, and with a job definition that was not manifested again, it ends as completed with ERROR: RAG ingestion failed: … as the last message of the program in its log.
documents.s: After an upgrade: manifest every setup once

documents.t: The RAG Builder is not an application of its own. It is the RAG setup kind of the Prompt Builder: the same single-file app, the same job definition (/SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/Prompt Builder/SAS-LLM-Prompt-Builder-UI) and the same Data-Driven Content object in the Prompt Builder report. There is nothing to build and no job definition to create for it — deploy the Prompt Builder as described in Deploying the Builder UIs, then switch RAG on: Import the package or deploy the runtime (above), so the content root holds rag_core, the steps, the jobs and the model template. Open the Prompt Builder report, select the object and open its Options pane. The release table Public.ACCELERATOR_RELEASES has to be assigned to the object, as for every use of it — see step 5. Tick Enable RAG setups. The options that start with RAG: appear below the checkbox. Fill them in: the embedding model project, the content root, the CAS server, the ingestion compute context, a checkbox per vector database the deployment offers, and the operational policy (TLS, deleted-document handling, history retention, run-history recording, embedding replicas, table persistence). The Model Manager repository, the SCR endpoint, the deployment type and the credential domain are the ones the Prompt Builder already has; they are set once and used by every kind. The whole list, with defaults, is in Configuration. The Setup card of the Prompt Builder then offers RAG setup for a document collection beside the template kinds, and choosing it shows the Builder's own four steps. While the switch is not ticked — the default — the kind is not offered, nothing of the Builder is loaded and nothing RAG is requested from SAS Viya. With it enabled, the first request for RAG is made when a user chooses the kind. The policy values are recorded onto each setup as it is created, so a setup keeps what it was built with. Three settings worth checking when RAG does not behave as expected The credential domain must not be none. Prompt and decision templates read none as "look no key up". RAG has no such mode — the ingestion and the retrieval take the store's user, password, host and database from the domain — so the RAG card is shown disabled and says why. The Model Manager repository ID must be set. Every kind needs it; without it the kind is not offered. The ingestion compute context is not the optimization compute context. The option is ragComputeContext (RAG: ingestion compute context); the option computeContext belongs to the prompt optimization job and is never read for an ingestion. A blank ragComputeContext does not hide the kind: it blocks Launch ingestion and Test retrieval with a message that names the setting. These options live inside the report Importing a newer Prompt Builder report from a transfer package replaces every value above with whatever the package was built against — silently, since the report still opens and the app still runs, with RAG switched off. Save them with mdb options-save before importing and restore them after: see Preserving builder options across a report import. That section also covers a site that still has the retired report named RAG Builder from release 2.2 or earlier. Served standalone rather than embedded, the same settings are query parameters of the Prompt Builder job — the switch included, because it is off by default: .../SASJobExecution/?_program=/SAS Agentic AI Accelerator/Prompt Builder/SAS-LLM-Prompt-Builder-UI&_action=form&enableRag=true&modelRepositoryID=<uuid>&embeddingProjectID=<uuid>&ragComputeContext=<context name> (The browser encodes the blanks.) Without an LLM project in the URL the page shows the RAG Builder alone; add llmProjectID and SCREndpoint to get the template kinds beside it. A URL written for the job definition RAG-Builder-UI of release 2.2 or earlier has to be rewritten this way: that definition is retired, its context parameter was called computeContext, and it needed no enableRag. id is no longer read from the URL. For your own builds: npm run build:rag is gone, and npm run build produces the one dist/index.html that holds all three kinds. If you replace the app by hand: the HTML is the FORM, and the form is a property mdb builders-import and the manual steps in Deploying the Builder UIs put the built dist/index.html into the job definition for you. Updating the definition through the REST API instead has two ways to go wrong, both of which look like something else: &_action=form serves the job's form. HTML in code produces "Parameter Error — HTML form file was not found", which reads like a missing file rather than the wrong field. The form is an entry inside the definition's properties list, named form — not a top-level form key. A PUT carrying a top-level key returns 200 and silently drops it, so the deploy looks successful while the old app keeps serving. Verify by reading the property back, not by trusting the status code. What the Builder never asks a user Three things a person building a corpus should not have to know are resolved rather than typed: Comes from Vector store host, port, database The credential domain — see below Embedding model Listed from the embedding model project Embedding dimensions The chosen model's fact sheet Maximum chunk size Capped at the chosen model's published token window A typed model name has nothing behind it until a container is published, and the failure surfaces as an HTTP 404 at the first embed call — after the crawl and the chunking have already run. A vector column is created at the model's width and cannot be widened afterwards. And text beyond a model's token window is dropped by the model silently rather than rejected, so an oversized chunk is embedded from its opening only — retrieval then matches on text the answer never sees, with nothing in the run reporting a problem. The Builder asks for the model first for that reason: the ceiling has to be known before anyone picks a chunk size under it.

Button What it leaves in your environment Save setup The RAG Setup model in SAS Model Manager Manifest setup Saves, then the ingestion job definition and the Studio flow in the Generated artifacts folder, retrieve_context.py as the setup's score code, and a new minor model version Launch ingestion A job run, the collection, and the pipeline tables in the chosen caslib Browse ledger Nothing — reads the promoted ledger table Test retrieval Nothing. See below Test retrieval asks the live collection a question and shows the chunks that come back, with what the probe cost. It is deliberately built to leave no trace: the job definition it runs is created without a parent folder, so it never appears anywhere in SAS Content, and it is deleted when the run ends — including when the run fails or is abandoned. The hits travel back in the job log rather than in a CAS table, because an output table would itself be an artifact of a test meant to have none. The finished job's own record and log remain in SAS Job Execution, as for any job run. It exercises the collection, not the registered score code: it queries through rag_core exactly as the ingestion does, so a broken retrieve_context.py would still pass. Verifying that needs the published model.
documents.s: What the Builder's buttons create — and what they clean up

documents.t: Manifest setup generates two things that ingest the same setup: the ingestion job, which is the one program Ingest-Documents.sas, and the SAS Studio flow, which is made of the RAG custom steps. Both keep the same ledger, <prefix>_LEDGER, and both take the same run lock on it: a row that the start of a run appends to the table. They do not store the ledger alike: The ledger was last written by Its text columns are the ingestion job CHAR, with fixed lengths the flow (RAG - Load Vector Store), or RAG - Purge Documents VARCHAR CAS does not append a row whose column is VARCHAR where the table has CHAR, or the other way round. Up to release 2.2 each of the two declared its lock row the one way it stores the ledger itself. Seen on 2026-10-11 on SAS Viya 2026.09: a setup ingested with Launch ingestion, then its generated flow run in SAS Studio, stopped in the first step with ERROR: The variable doc_id has been specified with incompatible data types. ERROR: The action stopped due to errors. ERROR: RAG - List Documents failed: the run lock could not be written to <caslib>.<prefix>_LEDGER - refusing to ingest unguarded and left the ledger as it was. The append the other way round — a CHAR row to a VARCHAR table, which is the job on a ledger a flow wrote — was refused with the same text in a scratch caslib. The job itself was not run on a ledger a flow had written before the change; by its code it did not look whether its lock had been written, so it would have gone on without one. From release 2.3.0 the job, RAG - List Documents and RAG - Purge Documents ask the table for its column types (table.columnInfo) before they take the lock, and declare the lock row the way the table holds its text. The log of the run says which it found: NOTE: the ledger … holds its text columns as char - the run lock is written the same way, or as varchar. The steps that read the ledger compare its values without the blanks a CHAR column is padded with. Nothing has to be migrated: a ledger of either type is used as it is, and it still changes its type with the writer that last completed a run. The two were not made to store the ledger alike; that would have changed how the last step of a flow, or the job, writes the table, and neither change could be measured. The new lock is in the steps and in the job, which reach a site with the transfer package, or from a checkout with deploy-rag-content. The job definition of a setup holds a copy of Ingest-Documents.sas as it was when the setup was manifested, so manifest the setup again afterwards; whether a flow generated earlier runs the redeployed steps without that was not checked. Measured on 2026-10-11 on SAS Viya 2026.09, with the ingestion job and the generated flow of one setup, in both directions: The job on the ledger it had written (CHAR). The log said NOTE: the ledger Public.…_LEDGER holds its text columns as char - the run lock is written the same way, the append added one row, and the run completed with 3 documents unchanged. The generated flow on that CHAR ledger — the case that had failed with incompatible data types. All five steps ended green. Afterwards the ledger was VARCHAR, with 3 rows of status unchanged and no lock row. The job on the VARCHAR ledger the flow had left. The log said … holds its text columns as varchar - the run lock is written the same way, the append added one row, and the run completed with 3 unchanged. Measured again on 2026-10-11 on the same system, with pgvector and with SingleStore 9.0.40. The job and the flows ran as SAS Job Execution jobs in the SAS Studio compute context, the flows as the code SAS Studio generates for them and not clicked in SAS Studio, on ledgers in CASUSER: A project without a ledger, then the job twice. The first run found 3 documents new, and the ledger it wrote was CHAR. The second run logged as char, appended the lock and completed with 3 unchanged. The same on SingleStore. The step RAG - Purge Documents in the mode purge, on a CHAR and on a VARCHAR ledger (pgvector), and on a CHAR ledger (SingleStore). The step logged the type it found and appended its lock, its log said removed 1 chunk rows for 1 documents, and the ledger held 2 documents afterwards and no lock row. The ingestion that followed — the flow in two of the three cases, the job in one — found the purged document as new and brought it back. On pgvector the removed chunk row is the step's own log line; on SingleStore the collection was read and held 2 chunks. A first step that fails and hands the lock back, on both types (pgvector). RAG - List Documents with a documents folder that does not exist appended its lock, failed, and wrote NOTE: RAG - List Documents: the run lock was released so the run can be retried. The ledger kept its 3 rows and its type and held no lock row, and the next run, less than three minutes later, was not refused. The job reads its lock back (see below). Every job run on a ledger that existed showed two PROC JSON steps before the Python program and completed. Not measured in those runs: a lock that CAS refuses, which is what the read-back of the job is there for; a first run of the flow without a ledger with these steps (a flow on a ledger of its own ran green earlier the same day, before the change); the fallback for a table whose column types cannot be read; two runs at the same time, and with them a run that the lock of another run refuses; and a lock older than 30 minutes. What the job does with its lock when its run fails was not measured either. By the code of that day it left its lock row in the ledger; it now takes its own row out again. All of these but the first and the third were measured later the same day, with the job and the steps as release 2.3.0 ships them — see Measured with the runtime of release 2.3.0 at the end of this section. The job reads its lock back. RAG - List Documents reads the lock it appended and refuses to go on without one. The job did not: by its code a lock that CAS had refused went unnoticed there, and the job went on without one. It now exports the ledger a second time, after the append, and looks for a lock row the first export did not hold. Without one it ends with RAG ingestion failed: RuntimeError: the run lock could not be written to the ledger … - refusing to ingest unguarded, and the ledger stays as it was. The check sees only that the row is not there, so the message names where to look and not one cause: the SAS log above it, for an ERROR of the append or of the export after it. The passing case was measured, as said above; the refusal was not provoked. To see it on a site: run the job of a setup whose ledger exists (Launch ingestion after deploy-rag-content and Manifest setup) — the run has to complete as before, and its log then shows two PROC JSON steps before the Python program where it showed one. What follows in this section was written after those measurements. It is in the steps and in the job of release 2.3.0 and was run on the same system later that day: Measured with the runtime of release 2.3.0, at the end of this section, says what was seen and what was not run. The test suite of rag_core holds the text of the macros and runs the Python of the job. Who hands a lock back. A step that fails hands the run lock back by rewriting the ledger without that row — copy, drop, promote, save — and then writes a NOTE that begins with its name and says the run lock was released so the run can be retried. The steps measured above did that whether the run held a lock or not. Seen in those runs: a purge that had gone through, a preview of a purge and a RAG - Register Setup that failed after RAG - Load Vector Store had already written the ledger each rewrote the ledger once more and wrote the NOTE. A run that the lock of another run had refused did the same by the code, and saved the ledger with the lock row of the other run in it. Now only a failing run whose own lock row stands in the ledger rewrites it and writes the NOTE. A run that another run's lock refused and a step that fails after the ledger was written leave the ledger alone, a purge that went through has written the ledger without its lock row and does not write it a second time, and none of them says that a lock was released. A preview of RAG - Purge Documents takes no lock at all (retention and erasure). The job hands its lock back. Up to this change the job appended its lock row before its Python program looked for the lock of another run, and only a run that went through took the row out again, by storing the ledger. A run that failed left a fresh lock row behind, and a run that another lock had refused left a second one. The next run of the job or of the flow was then refused for 30 minutes with nothing running: another ingestion run appears active for this ledger (run lock held) - retry later. The row carried no run id, so nothing could tell it from the lock of another run. The job now makes its run id in SAS, as RAG - List Documents does, and writes it into the lock row. It looks for a fresh lock of another run before it appends; a run that is refused appends nothing, exports the ledger once and leaves the table and its saved file as they are. SAS refuses such a run before the Python program looks, so the message ends the run as it stands above, without RuntimeError: in front of it. A run that failed after it took the lock copies the ledger without the row that carries its own id, drops the table, promotes and saves the copy, and writes NOTE: RAG ingestion: the run lock was released so the run can be retried. The ledger keeps its column types. A lock row with an empty run id — written by a job definition that was not manifested again — is the lock of another run to the job and to the steps: it refuses while it is less than 30 minutes old, is ignored afterwards, and stays in the ledger until a run that goes through writes it. One limit, read from the code and not measured. A lock row carries the time of the SAS clock, and the Python programs of the job and of the steps compare it with their own clock, which is UTC. In a compute session whose SAS clock is not UTC — the option TIMEZONE — the two differ by the offset. East of UTC the Python program of the job then still takes for fresh a lock row that SAS took for stale: such a run has appended its own lock, hands it back, and its message does carry RuntimeError:. The sessions of the test system run in UTC. More than one lock row. A run that crashes leaves its lock row behind; 30 minutes later the next run ignores it and appends its own beside it, and the stale row stays until a run that goes through writes the ledger. The job and the steps RAG - List Documents, RAG - Load Vector Store and RAG - Purge Documents take the newest lock row to decide whether another run holds the lock. They took one row, whichever CAS returned first or last, so a stale row could hide the lock of a run that was at work. No such ledger had come about on the test system by itself; the measurement below made one. The job ends as failed when the run failed. Ingest-Documents.sas never raises a SAS error, so up to release 2.2 SAS Job Execution reported every run of it as completed and the outcome was in the log only. The program now sets SYSCC as its last statement when the run failed, and SAS Job Execution then reports the job as failed. It still runs to its last statement; nothing aborts. That statement was measured for the job RAG - Register Setup generates from a flow, which ended as failed (the job generated from a flow), and later the same day for Ingest-Documents.sas (below). Two ways out of the program used to leave no milestone for the Prompt Builder either: a saved ledger that cannot be loaded, and a compute context without the requests package. Both now write the milestone Ingestion failed: … that every other failure writes, so Launch ingestion shows The ingestion run did not succeed where it showed Run finished. The ingestion ledger is below. The job stores a ledger only after a run that went through. The job stored rag_ledger_out.json whenever that file existed in WORK. In a SAS session that had run the job before, a later run that stopped early found the file of the earlier run and stored that ledger again, over the saved file. A job started by SAS Job Execution has a WORK of its own and was not affected. The two files the job reads the ledger and its lock from, rag_ledger_in.json and rag_ledger_lock.json, stayed in WORK as well: in a SAS session that had run the job before, a run that found no ledger in memory exported none and read the two files of the earlier run — that ledger as its own, and its lock as the lock that was written. The job now deletes both before it exports anything and says so (NOTE: RAG ingestion: rag_ledger_in.json of an earlier run of this SAS session was deleted from WORK); a file that is there and cannot be deleted stops the run. The line is written for each of the two files that is there: for both after a run that took a lock, for rag_ledger_in.json alone after a run that was refused, and for none after a run that had no ledger. The run id. A run is named run-<epoch>-<ten digits>, and rag_runs is keyed on that name and shared by every project in the database. The digits were &sysjobid in the steps and the process id in the job, and neither told two sessions apart: twelve flow runs of the measurements above, each in a compute server of its own, ended in -344, the four other runs with an id a step had made in -343 or -345, and the job runs in -400 to -408. Two runs that started in the same second could therefore get the same id; no such collision was seen. The steps and the job now take the ten digits from a UUID, in SAS (&sysjobid only where UUIDGEN returns nothing); the lock row of the job carries the id. The Python program of the job makes an id with ten random digits only where SAS hands it none. Ids written before keep their form and are read as before. The epoch in the id is the time of the SAS clock — in the steps as before, and now in the job, whose Python program made the id from its own clock up to release 2.2. What that means for started_at is said under run history. Measured with the runtime of release 2.3.0, on 2026-10-11 on SAS Viya 2026.09 with pgvector, in the SAS Studio compute context. The job ran in SAS Job Execution and, where one SAS session had to hold several runs, as a program in a compute session. The flows ran as the code SAS Studio generates for them and were not clicked in SAS Studio. The lock of another run was that of a flow that really ran; the old and the stale lock rows were appended by hand. A job run that fails after it took the lock, on a CHAR and on a VARCHAR ledger, with one parameter of the configuration changed. The log held, in this order: NOTE: the ledger … holds its text columns as char - the run lock is written the same way (or as varchar); the append of one row; NOTE: Python-Subprocess - RAGINGEST Ingestion failed: RuntimeError: configuration drift: …; a table <ledger>_R with the 4 rows the ledger had before the run, its promote and its save; NOTE: RAG ingestion: the run lock was released so the run can be retried; and ERROR: RAG ingestion failed: RuntimeError: configuration drift: …. The ledger then held the same 4 document rows, no lock row and the column type it had. The job run again five seconds later was not refused and completed. A job launched while the flow of the same ledger runs. No append and one PROC JSON step; the milestone Ingestion failed: another ingestion run appears active for this ledger (run lock held) - retry later and the same text behind ERROR: RAG ingestion failed:, without RuntimeError:; no <ledger>_R and no line about a released lock. The ledger held one lock row, the flow's, and its saved file kept its size and time. The flow completed, and the job run again five seconds after it was not refused. A flow started while another flow of the same ledger runs ended in RAG - List Documents with ERROR: RAG - List Documents failed: another ingestion run holds the lock on this ledger - wait for it to finish, or retry in 30 minutes if it crashed. Its log held no rewrite of the ledger and no line about a released lock, the ledger kept the lock row of the first flow, and that flow completed. The lock row carries the run id. Read from another session while a job ran, the ledger held one row __run_lock__ with the status lock and the run_id of the milestone RAGINGEST run run-…: ledger has 4 documents, config …, which is also the id of the run in rag_runs. A lock row with an empty run id, as a job definition from before release 2.3.0 writes it. 60 seconds old, it refused the job and the flow, and it was still the only lock row afterwards. Older than 30 minutes, it was ignored: the job logged RAGINGEST stale run lock ignored (held > 30 minutes), the steps NOTE: RAG - List Documents: a stale run lock (held longer than 30 minutes) is ignored and RAGLIST stale run lock ignored (held longer than 30 minutes). A job run that failed kept it — <ledger>_R held 5 rows, the 4 documents and that row — and a run that went through left a ledger without lock rows. A job run that fails at the configuration drift does not write the line about the stale lock: the drift is looked at first. Two lock rows, a stale one and a fresh one with the id of another run, appended in either order: the job and RAG - List Documents were refused both ways and left both rows. With a flow that ran beside a stale row, the job and a second flow launched while it ran were refused. CAS does not fix the order of the rows of a table; what was varied is the order of the two appends. A step hands a lock back only when it holds one. A failing RAG - List Documents took its own row out and wrote the NOTE, on both column types, and the run after it was not refused. A RAG - Register Setup that failed after RAG - Load Vector Store and a purge that went through did not rewrite the ledger a second time and wrote no such NOTE. The job ends as failed. The nine job runs that failed ended as failed in SAS Job Execution after 16.5 to 20 seconds, the eight that went through as completed. The record of a failed job holds the error code 5713 of SAS Job Execution, A procedure in the SAS program provided for the job completed execution with at least one error., and inside it an error with the code 1012 and the text of the program's ERROR line. That line is the last message of the program, not the last line of the log: the timing lines of its DATA step and the echoed source of the last statement follow it. The job stores no ledger after a run that was refused, in a SAS session that had run it to success before: behind the Python program the log held no promote and no save, and the ledger, its saved file and the lock row of the running flow were as before. The exports of an earlier run. In one SAS session, a run for a second setup that had no ledger wrote the two NOTE lines, ran no PROC JSON step, logged ledger has 0 documents and found its documents new. No job started by SAS Job Execution wrote the lines. With rag_ledger_in.json replaced by a directory that held a file, the run ended with … could not be deleted from WORK - stopped, because the run would read the ledger of that run as its own. Above the milestone of that run stood three ERROR messages of PROC JSON, on six log lines: the export still runs after the delete failed (see troubleshooting). The run id. Every id ended in ten digits — 28 ids in the logs of the flows, the purges and the job of one pass, 15 of the job in another — and no two endings were alike. The ledger held the 25 characters of the id, and rag_runs.started_at was the time the id names. Launched from the Prompt Builder page of this release. Launch ingestion of a setup on this runtime ended as completed, with run ids of the form run-<epoch>-<ten digits> and the run history recorded. Three runs of one setup showed 6 documents new, then 6 changed, then 6 unchanged and 1 new. Not run, and as the code and the tests have it: a job run that fails because a saved ledger cannot be loaded, with its milestone (see the next section); the lock that CAS refuses, which the read-back of the job is there for; the fallback for a table whose column types cannot be read; the texts the Prompt Builder shows for a run that failed — the page was not opened on one; a run that slips in between the steps of a flow that is running; a lock row left by a job definition of an earlier release that really failed; an export of an earlier run that cannot be deleted for another reason than being a directory; and a compute session whose SAS clock is not UTC.
documents.s: One ledger for the job and the flow

documents.t: The pipeline promotes and saves <project>_LEDGER and <project>_EMBEDDED. Up to release 2.2 every reader looked only at the table in memory and nothing loaded the saved file. After a restart of the CAS server — or for any ledger that was never loaded again — RAG - List Documents therefore found no ledger, started one that held only its run lock and classified the whole corpus as new: every chunk went through the enrichment prompts and the embedding model again, and the saved ledger was overwritten with the result. From release 2.3.0 the saved table is loaded before it is read, by one macro that is worded the same in all seven programs: Program Loads back RAG - List Documents, RAG - Purge Documents, RAG - Register Setup, Ingest-Documents.sas <project>_LEDGER RAG - Embed Chunks, RAG - Enrich Chunks <project>_EMBEDDED RAG - Load Vector Store both The log then says NOTE: RAG: <caslib>.<table> was saved but not in memory and has been loaded from its saved file. The .sashdat is matched by name without regard to case. With the run lock above, the order is: load the saved table back, ask it for its column types, append the lock, read the lock back. What the macro finds decides how the run goes on: The macro finds The run the table in memory goes on with it; a table in memory is never replaced by its saved copy no table in memory and no saved file starts as before, without a previous run a saved file, and loads it goes on with the loaded table and writes the NOTE above. A load that a concurrent run got to first is not an error a saved file that cannot be loaded fails, before it takes a lock or starts a ledger: the saved table … could not be loaded into memory (CAS messages above) - stopped, because an empty table would re-embed the corpus and overwrite the saved file. In the job the Python program writes the milestone Ingestion failed: the saved table … and returns, and the job ends as failed no table in memory, and the files of the caslib cannot be listed goes on without the table, with two WARNING lines The last row is the case the reload is there for, without the reload: where the ledger is not in memory, every document counts as new, the corpus is embedded again and the saved file is overwritten. The run does not stop there, because a caslib that cannot be listed says nothing about whether a saved copy exists; it says what it does: WARNING: RAG: <caslib>.<table> is not in memory, and the files of the caslib <caslib> could not be listed (CAS messages above) - a saved copy could not be looked for. WARNING: RAG: the run continues without the table and saves over a copy that may be there. A ledger that is not in memory means that every document counts as new and is embedded again. When PROC CAS ends before it says what it found, not even that much is known, and the first line reads WARNING: RAG: could not look for … - PROC CAS ended before it said whether the table is in memory or saved (messages above). The run continues with what is in memory. Up to this change both cases wrote one NOTE, could not look for a saved copy of …, which no longer exists. The two WARNING lines, the milestone of the job and the failed state of the job were written after the first measurements below. The wording of the two WARNING lines and the failed state of the job were measured later that day; a saved file that cannot be loaded, with the milestone of the job for it, was not run in SAS — see the end of this section. Measured on 2026-10-11 on SAS Viya 2026.09, with pgvector, with the saved tables dropped from memory while their .sashdat files stayed — the CAS server was not restarted: The job, on a CHAR and on a VARCHAR ledger: the log held the NOTE for <project>_LEDGER, the lock was appended with the type of the loaded table, and the run found 3 documents unchanged and embedded nothing. The flow, on a CHAR and on a VARCHAR ledger: RAG - List Documents loaded the ledger back, appended its lock and listed 3 documents as unchanged; RAG - Embed Chunks loaded <project>_EMBEDDED back and found nothing to embed. Measured again later that day, with the runtime of release 2.3.0 (pgvector, the saved ledger dropped from memory): the job and RAG - List Documents wrote the NOTE, loaded the ledger and found every document unchanged. And for the last row of the table, in RAG - List Documents with the ledger in a caslib of the CAS session whose files CAS could not list: the log held the two WARNING messages above, word for word, on four log lines below the CAS errors. That run did not reach its end. The step went on to its run lock, and a caslib of a session cannot hold the promoted table the lock is appended to, so it stopped with the run lock could not be written to … - refusing to ingest unguarded. Whether a run in a global caslib whose files cannot be listed ends, and what it saves, is not measured: the user of the test may add no path caslib. Not run: a saved file that cannot be loaded. No file that CAS cannot load could be put into a caslib of the test. The compute server does not see the directory of the caslib, CAS refuses to save another format under a .sashdat name (ERROR: Save exportoptions file type and name extension do not match.), and the caslibs whose directories the compute server does see belong to other people. So the CAS errors of such a load, the ERROR of the step, the milestone Ingestion failed: the saved table … of the job and the untouched file are as the code and the tests have them. What a run of the job leaves behind that stops before it takes a lock was measured for a run that another lock refused: no lock row, no store, the saved file untouched (one ledger for the job and the flow). Not measured: a restart of the CAS server; a saved file that cannot be loaded; a global caslib whose files cannot be listed; the reload in RAG - Purge Documents, RAG - Register Setup and RAG - Enrich Chunks, which did not run in that state (RAG - Enrich Chunks did not run at all); the reload of RAG - Load Vector Store itself, because both tables were in memory again by the time it ran; and SingleStore. The About tabs of those four steps name the reload and claim no measurement for it. The test suite of rag_core holds the text of the macro, its place in every program and the order with the run lock. A job definition holds a copy of Ingest-Documents.sas from the day the setup was manifested, so the job of a setup loads its ledger back only once Manifest setup has run again after deploy-rag-content. Anything that reads the ledger outside the steps and the job — the ledger view of the Builder, for one — still sees no ledger after a restart until a run has loaded it, and <project>_ELEMENTS and <project>_CHUNKS are saved and not loaded back.
documents.s: A saved ledger is loaded back

documents.t: The documents of a collection and the question asked of it have to be embedded by the same container: a question embedded somewhere else searches the collection with the wrong vectors, and nothing reports it. The Builder therefore resolves the embedding endpoint of a setup once — the SCR endpoint option of the Prompt Builder object, and <SAS Viya host>/llm where that option is blank, the host being the SAS Viya host option or the address the page is opened at — and gives the same value to everything it generates and starts. (A stored setup that names an endpoint of its own, embedding.scrEndpoint, keeps it ahead of the option; the Builder itself never writes one.) Receives it as The ingestion job, at Manifest setup and at Launch ingestion the parameter scrEndpoint The Embed step of the generated SAS Studio flow the step option _rgem_scrEndpoint Test retrieval the parameter scrEndpoint The retrieval model the constant EMBED_ENDPOINT in its MANIFEST block With a blank option, that address has to be reachable from the compute session of the ingestion and from the destination the retrieval model is published to. Where the page is opened under a name that is not — a port-forward, an alias of a reverse proxy — set the SCR endpoint option. The value is written at Manifest setup. A job definition, a flow and a retrieval model generated earlier keep what they were generated with until the setup is manifested again; a launch from the page always passes the current value, a scheduled run of the job and a run of the flow in SAS Studio do not. The retrieval model looks for the endpoint in this order and takes the first that is not blank: scr_endpoint in the options input of the call, the environment variable RAGEMBED_ENDPOINT on the destination, the manifested EMBED_ENDPOINT, SAS_SERVICES_URL + /llm, where the variable is set — a compute session sets it. Up to release 2.2 the fourth came before the third, so in a compute session the question was embedded at <SAS Viya host>/llm whatever the setup had been manifested for. The order is part of retrieve_context.py: a model has it once deploy-rag-content has published the current template and the setup has been manifested again.

The retrieval model — registered by Manifest setup of the Builder, or by the custom step RAG - Register Setup in SAS Studio — makes two HTTPS calls itself: to the embedding container, to embed the question, and — only in a compute session, where a session token exists — to the credentials service. It verifies both against the CA bundle of the deployment, and two environment variables per call decide how: Call CA bundle Verification on or off Embedding container RAGEMBED_CABUNDLE RAGEMBED_SSLVERIFY Credentials service RAGSTORE_CABUNDLE RAGSTORE_SSLVERIFY <prefix>_CABUNDLE names the bundle and defaults to /security/trustedcerts.pem. When that file does not exist where the model runs, the model verifies against the certificates Python trusts by default, and a certificate signed by the deployment's own CA is refused. <prefix>_SSLVERIFY set to false, no or 0 switches verification off on that destination; set to true, yes or 1 it switches verification on. The variable wins in both directions. When the variable is not set, or holds any other word, the constant SSL_VERIFY in the MANIFEST block of the model decides. The Builder writes it from the option Verify TLS certificates in manifested models (sslVerify) of the Prompt Builder object: True while the option is ticked, which is the default, and False while it is not. The custom step RAG - Register Setup writes it from a checkbox of its own, in the same way — see the checkbox of the custom step. So the option is a default written when the setup is manifested.
