could not be given to the linked table, which has none now. (link) CAS refused the label. The links are in the table Many rows with match_method = none Expected for direct calls of a model, for the health check of a prompt optimization, for queries whose prompt does not follow within _lnk_query_window seconds and for embeddings outside of an ingestion run. For the calls of a published prompt or decision: look whether MODEL_CATALOG holds its template (role = prompt or decision, runID empty) and whether the template has 20 characters of fixed text - the link program counts the templates that have less in a NOTE. For the calls of an optimization or of a judge: look whether the catalog holds rows of the role optimization or judge for the prompt, with the model the calls went to in target_model Rows with match_method = ambiguous Two callers fit equally well: two prompts or decision templates with the same text, one question asked of two collections in the same second, two RAG setups with one collection of which neither is the registration of the other, two ingestion runs that overlap, a run table that several setups share. match_candidates is their number
documents.s: The log table, the pull and the link: what their messages mean

documents.t: This part of the troubleshooting guide describes issues that can occur when publishing decisions or models that call the LLMs to a SAS Container Runtime (SCR) publishing destination (independent of AWS, Azure, GCP or Private Docker).

This error is mostly likely caused by the fact that you are using a certificate for the LLM containers that isn't valid according other SCR containers - this might be because you are using a self-signed certificate or organization signed. This fix has to be done by the person that deploys the container - for more information check out the SAS documentation: --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: <CONTAINER> namespace: <NS> spec: selector: matchLabels: app: <APP_NAME> template: metadata: labels: app: <APP_NAME> spec: containers: - name: <APP_NAME> image: <CONTAINER_REGISTRY>/<CONTAINER>:latest resources: requests: memory: "4000Mi" cpu: "1000m" ports: - containerPort: 8080 protocol: TCP env: - name: SAS_SCR_SSL_CERTIFICATE value: /ssl/certificate-file.crt ... Shortend for brevity Please note that you have to mount the certificate file in a volume to the container!
documents.s: SSL Error: Missing CA trust list

documents.t: The User Guide describes the tools you work with once an administrator has deployed the SAS Agentic AI Accelerator - see the Administration Guide for that part. Model Definition Builder - add an LLM or embedding model to the environment with one definition.yaml and the mdb command line, check it locally, and register and publish it to SAS Model Manager and the SAS Container Runtime. Prompt Builder - test a prompt across several LLMs at once, let a judge model rank the responses, keep a versioned experiment history in SAS Model Manager, optimize the prompt with DSPy, and turn the best prompt into a scoreable model for SAS Intelligent Decisioning. The same tool designs decision templates for decision models and, as its third kind, RAG setups - the RAG Builder is part of it. RAG - turn a folder of documents into a governed vector-store collection with the RAG custom steps or with a RAG setup in the Prompt Builder, ask it questions, and publish the retrieval as a model a decision can call. The SAS code, custom steps and Python samples behind these tools are listed in the repository's SAS Viya Integrations and Non-SAS Viya Integrations folders.

The Model Definition Builder (mdb) is the fastest way to add a new LLM or embedding model to the framework. Instead of copying an existing model folder and editing ten files by hand, you describe the model once and mdb generates every asset the framework needs — consistently and reproducibly. This guide walks through creating, checking and iterating on a model. For the operations view (CI drift gates, deployment YAML, air-gapped installs, the option vocabulary), see the Model Definition Builder administration guide.

Every model is described by a single definition.yaml in its folder — the only file you edit. From it, mdb renders the score script, inputVar.json/outputVar.json, modelConfiguration.json, options.json, requirements.json, the documentation files and the model's row in the fact sheet. Because they all come from one source, the three-way drift between score code, options and fact sheet that used to creep into hand-written definitions simply cannot happen. When you want to change something, you edit definition.yaml and re-generate.

cd Model-Definition-Builder/cli python -m venv .venv .venv/Scripts/activate # Windows; on Linux/macOS: source .venv/bin/activate pip install -e ".[viya]" mdb --help Python 3.11 or newer. The [viya] extra (keep the quotes - some shells expand the brackets) adds sasctl, which every command that registers, publishes or configures SAS Viya needs; plain pip install -e . is enough to add, generate, validate and test definitions locally. Provider API keys and your Viya connection are read from a .env file at the repository root (copy .env.example and fill it in) — keys are never written into any generated file.

Run mdb add from anywhere inside the repository. The wizard asks you to pick a provider, then a model from that provider's live (or bundled) catalog, then a few questions, and shows you exactly what it will create before writing anything: mdb add Prefer a one-liner? Every answer has a flag, so the same thing works non-interactively: # A hosted model through a provider API mdb add openai gpt-4o-mini --id gpt_4o_mini --yes mdb add anthropic claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 --id claude_sonnet_4_5 --yes # Azure AI Foundry, addressed by your deployment name mdb add azure-foundry --resource myres --deployment my-gpt41 --id gpt_41_az --yes # A model you host yourself on Hugging Face weights (downloaded into the image) mdb add hf-selfhosted --repo Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct --id qwen_25_05b --params-billions 0.5 --yes mdb picks the provider, model version, endpoint, requirements and applicable options for you. When you pick a reasoning model, for example, it offers reasoning_effort instead of temperature/top_p, because those models reject them.

LLM-Definitions/gpt_4o_mini/ definition.yaml # the only file you edit gpt4oMiniScore.py # generated score script inputVar.json outputVar.json modelConfiguration.json options.json requirements.json README.md Model-Card.md Open definition.yaml — it is short and readable. Everything else is derived from it.

Two quick checks catch most problems locally: mdb validate gpt_4o_mini --live # coherence rules + one real provider call mdb test gpt_4o_mini # run the generated scoreModel() with a prompt validate --live sends a single smoke-test request to the provider (using the key from your .env), so you know the model answers before you register it. test runs the generated score code exactly as SAS Viya will.
documents.s: Check it before it touches SAS Viya

documents.t: Change anything in definition.yaml, then regenerate. For example, to raise the default max_tokens and add a seed: options: temperature: default: 0.7 max_tokens: default: 2000 seed: default: 42 mdb generate gpt_4o_mini # re-render the generated files mdb sync gpt_4o_mini # update the fact-sheet row The options you can use — and how each maps to the provider — are defined centrally; see scoring-time options for the full list, and custom options if you need a provider-specific parameter that is not in the standard set.

Embedding models work exactly like LLMs — mdb puts them in Embedding-Definitions/ and keeps embedding_fact_sheet.csv in step. Several open-source embedding models are bundled and run on CPU, including the RTEB-leaderboard IBM Granite models: # Open-source, self-hosted on Hugging Face weights, runs on CPU mdb add hf-selfhosted --repo ibm-granite/granite-embedding-small-english-r2 \ --runtime sentence-transformers --id granite_embedding_small_r2 --yes After adding, open definition.yaml to set the correct Embedding_Length and Input_Token_Limit for the model, then mdb generate and mdb sync.

If you already run models on Ollama or vLLM, mdb can point a definition at that server for either chat or embeddings. The model weights stay on the server; the published container just calls it. The server URL is not baked in — it resolves at run time from the OLLAMA_BASE_URL / VLLM_BASE_URL environment variable (or a per-call option), so the same model works across your dev, test and production servers. # a chat model served by a local Ollama, addressed by its Ollama tag mdb add ollama llama3.1:8b --id llama31_8b_ollama --kind llm --yes # an embedding model served by vLLM, with the server URL baked as the default mdb add vllm nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 --id nomic_embed_vllm --kind embedding \ --base-url http://vllm-svc.ml.svc:8000/v1 --yes Set OLLAMA_BASE_URL / VLLM_BASE_URL (and an optional OLLAMA_API_KEY / VLLM_API_KEY) in your .env for local smoke tests, and in each deployment's environment to point at that environment's server.
documents.s: Use a self-hosted Ollama or vLLM server

documents.t: Once a model checks out, register and publish it from the CLI (needs the [viya] extra and your Viya connection in .env): mdb register gpt_4o_mini # create it in SAS Model Manager mdb publish gpt_4o_mini --wait # publish to SCR and wait for the image build On a brand-new environment you do not need any manual setup first — mdb register creates the model repository and the LLM/Embedding project if they do not exist yet (or run mdb setup up front). To update a model you already registered, edit definition.yaml, mdb generate, then mdb register gpt_4o_mini --update to replace it in place with a new version. mdb ship gpt_4o_mini does validate → register → publish in one step, and mdb unregister gpt_4o_mini removes a model from Model Manager again (the local folder is kept). The details are in Register, update and publish from the CLI. Publishing builds an SCR container image. Hosted-API, Ollama and vLLM models build in seconds (their image only needs requests). A self-hosted Hugging Face model bakes its weights into the image and installs PyTorch, so its build is heavier — mdb keeps it as lean as possible by installing the CPU-only PyTorch build (SCR runs on CPU) and downloading weights over HTTP, but very large models can still take a while. If a publish fails on a build timeout, that is the signal the image is too heavy for your environment's build limit.
documents.s: Register and publish to SAS Viya

documents.t: definition.yaml is the source of truth, so the loop is always the same: mdb generate <model_id> # re-render generated files from the manifest mdb sync <model_id> # update the fact-sheet row mdb validate <model_id> # cross-file coherence checks with fix-it hints mdb generate --all --check verifies that every generated file still matches its manifest; it is the CI gate that keeps the whole fleet honest. If you ever hand-edit a generated file, mdb notices and tells you to fold the change back into definition.yaml (or mark the file as hand-maintained) rather than overwriting your work silently.

Have a model folder from before mdb? Bring it under management without losing anything: mdb import <model_id> # writes definition.yaml, shows what would change mdb import <model_id> --apply # converges the folder onto the generated files The import lists every normalization it would apply so you can review the diff before committing, then re-test and re-publish.

Administration guide — CI drift gate, deployment YAML and CI recipes, air-gapped installs, the full option vocabulary, provider retirement radar LLM Definitions — the anatomy of a model definition, if you want to understand what mdb generates Register & Publish LLMs — the registration flow in depth

The LLM Prompt Builder is a no-code tool for prompt engineers. You test a prompt across several LLMs at once, compare the responses side by side, let an LLM judge which one is best, keep a versioned history of every experiment, and turn the winning prompt into a scoreable model you can use elsewhere on the platform — for example in SAS Intelligent Decisioning. Everything is saved in SAS Model Manager, so your work is governed and shareable. The same tool builds two more kinds of things, chosen on its first card under What are you building?: a decision template for decision models, and a RAG setup for a document collection. Which of them you see depends on what your administrator has switched on; where only prompt templates are offered, the question is not shown at all. This guide walks through using the tool, prompt templates first. For installing and embedding it in a SAS Visual Analytics report (and the one-time configuration a report author does), see Deploying the Builder UIs.

The page is a flow of steps, shown as a slim stepper across the top with Back and Continue beside it. Which steps it has depends on the kind you are building; for a prompt template they are: Step What you do there 1 Setup Choose the kind, where more than one is offered, then pick a project and a prompt-test — where this experiment history is stored in Model Manager. You do this once per session. 2 Build & Test The workbench, where the whole loop happens on one page: choose the LLMs and tune their options, set how responses are judged, write your prompt — a system prompt and a user prompt, with optional variables — run the experiment, then compare the responses in the tracker right below, mark the best response and save. 3 Optimize Only when your administrator has enabled prompt optimization: let DSPy rewrite the prompt from your Best Response runs. Without it the flow has three steps and Finalize is step 3. For a decision template this step is Evaluate instead (see Decision templates). 4 Finalize Manifest the best prompt — turn it into a scoreable model for the rest of the platform. Always the last step. You can open any step at any time by clicking it; nothing is locked, and only the step you are on is highlighted — steps are places to work in, not tasks that get ticked off, so revisit or skip them as you need. Editing, running and reading all stay on Build & Test: a finished run appears at the top of the tracker below the prompts, and loading an earlier run brings you back up to them; loading an optimized prompt from the Optimize step opens Build & Test for you. Every card explains itself in an Instructions box on its left; beside the tracker's instructions a summary counts your runs and those with a Best Response, and a legend explains the icons a run shows. A decision template keeps these steps with Evaluate in the place of Optimize; a RAG setup has four steps of its own — Setup, Documents & chunks, Store & output, Run & test — described under RAG setups. Nothing is sent to SAS Viya until you have the configuration in place, and no paid model call happens until you press Run Experiments.

At the top, choose an existing project or create one. A project is a Model Manager container that groups related prompt-tests; the Prompt Builder tags the ones it creates so they are easy to find. Inside a project you choose or create a prompt-test — this is the thing whose experiment history you are building. Both pickers are type-to-filter comboboxes — click one and start typing to narrow the open list live — and each additionally has a "created/modified by" filter, so long lists stay manageable. Use Create a new Project / Create a new Prompt to add them without leaving the tool. Both need a name with at least one character that can be seen. With the name field empty, or holding only what shows nothing — blanks, characters that Unicode marks as not displayed, such as a zero-width space, which a name pasted from elsewhere can bring along, control characters, or the braille pattern blank — nothing is sent to SAS Model Manager: the dialog says A project name is required. or A prompt name is required., marks the field and puts the cursor into it. Letters of any script, digits, punctuation and emoji all make a name. What is created is what stood in the dialog when you clicked; while the creation is out, the name and the description cannot be edited and the dialog cannot be closed — its buttons are disabled and Escape does nothing until SAS Model Manager has answered. If the creation is refused, or SAS Model Manager cannot be reached, the dialog stays open and says inside it what happened; nothing was created, and you can try again or close the dialog, with Escape as well. After a creation that went through, the dialog opens empty for the next one. The dialogs that create a RAG project and a RAG setup do the same. Should the page say after one of those two that a project or a setup was created but could not be listed or read back, it exists: use Try again rather than creating it a second time. Delete Prompt and Delete Project remove them again; before deleting, the tool checks whether any SAS Intelligent Decisioning decisions still use the prompt and warns you, so you do not break a running decision by accident. The confirmation lists those decisions, each with a link, or says that none was found, or says that the usage could not be verified — the prompt may then still be in use. If you open another prompt-test or choose another project while the tool is still checking, no confirmation comes up and nothing is deleted. A deletion that SAS Model Manager refuses says The deletion failed.; one whose request gets no usable answer is read back, as the paragraph on writes below says. Decision templates and RAG setups get the same note before they are deleted. The note is all that stands between the click and the deletion: SAS Model Manager does not refuse to delete a prompt that a decision still uses. The decision stays, and in SAS Intelligent Decisioning its model node then carries an error badge and Validate fails with NOT_FOUND for the model that is gone. Selecting a prompt-test loads its saved experiment runs into the Prompt Experiment Tracker on the Build & Test step, and brings the most recent run you marked as best straight into the workbench so you can carry on where you left off. If the documentation of a prompt-test could not be read, the documentation section says so and Save documentation stays off; choose another entry in the list and then the prompt-test again. A prompt-test that has no such run — a new one, above all — opens with the steps after Setup as they are on a page that was just loaded: empty prompts, no variables, no model selected, every option at its default, every explanation open or folded as it was then. The steps do not keep what the prompt-test before it had put there, in another project or after a change of kind either, and with no prompt-test open they show none; the same holds for a decision template and for a RAG setup. That includes what you typed into a prompt-test and did not save in a run: it goes when you open or create another one, without a question. What you typed into Build & Test or set on Optimize before any prompt-test was open is kept when you then create a prompt-test for it, or open one that has no best run; a prompt-test with a best run shows that run instead. An experiment, an evaluation or an optimization that is still running when you leave a prompt-test belongs to the one you left. The answers of an experiment or of an evaluation over a CAS table are dropped when they arrive, and the evaluation asks no further row. An optimization job goes on: its state, its run log and its result are shown on the prompt-test it runs for — also when you come back to it while it runs — and every other prompt-test only says An optimization is already running., which is why none can be started there. In a RAG setup, the chunks of a retrieval test and the state of an ingestion run are shown for the setup they were started for and for no other. The ingestion job itself goes on in SAS Viya. When you open its setup again, the Ingestion run card is back: the state of the job, its milestones and the time since the launch, and Launch ingestion stays off until the job has ended; a job that ended while another setup was open is shown as finished, with its ledger. On a page loaded after the launch, opening the setup asks SAS Job Execution for the runs of the setup's ingestion job that are pending or running, and shows the newest one the same way; Launch ingestion waits for that answer. If the state of the job cannot be read three times in a row, the card says that the run is no longer followed, and Launch ingestion can be used again. Look at the job in SAS Job Execution first: it may still be running. While the page writes to SAS Model Manager, you cannot change what is open. From the click on Save Experiments, Save documentation or Manifest Best Prompt (Manifest Best Decision Model on a decision template) until that write has ended, from the click on Run optimization until its job is launched, and from the confirmation of Compare targets…, of Delete Prompt, of Delete Project or of the delete of an optimization run, the controls of the Setup card are disabled: the cards under What are you building?, the project and prompt-test lists with their filters, the documentation fields, Create a new Project, Create a new Prompt and the two delete buttons. They can be used again as soon as the write has ended, whether it was saved, refused or failed, so what the page says about a write is said about the prompt-test that is open. The steps themselves stay reachable. The RAG Builder does the same for Save setup, Save documentation, Manifest setup, Delete setup and Delete project; its documentation fields stand on a card of their own and stay usable. Without this, a prompt-test opened right after a click on Save Experiments left the one that was being saved with a tracker that held no run. A change of the lists that a script sends meanwhile is undone, and a click a script sends to a control that is off - or to a node inside it, such as its text - reaches none of the page's listeners. A request that SAS Viya does not answer within two minutes is given up; the write then ends as one that failed, and the controls can be used again. The buttons that start a write stay off as long as any write is out, their own included: Save Experiments, Manifest Best Prompt, Run optimization, Compare targets… and the delete of an optimization run, and in the RAG Builder Save setup, Manifest setup and Save documentation. The RAG buttons are also off while a setup you have just opened is still being read. If it could not be read, the page says so, and they stay off until you open the setup again: choose another entry in the list and then the setup. After Create setup, a setup that could not be read back says the same in its warning, and Try again reads it. A rag-setup.json that SAS Model Manager answers with and that is no setup the page can read is named as such: repair or remove the file in SAS Model Manager. Launch ingestion and Run test are off while any write is out as well, so that no ingestion runs a job definition that Manifest setup is about to rewrite. Run test starts one test at a time: Enter in the question does nothing while a test runs, as the button does. Launch ingestion also waits while the page asks SAS Job Execution whether an ingestion of the setup is running - also when you open the setup twice and two questions are out. A Delete Project (or Delete project in the RAG Builder) that stops part of the way, because one of its prompt-tests or setups or the project itself is refused or gets no answer, reads the project back from SAS Model Manager: the list shows what is there, an item you had open that was deleted is closed, and the message names what was deleted and what is still in the project. A delete, a save or a creation whose request gets no usable answer - no answer at all, an error page of an ingress, a 502, 503 or 504 - is read back from SAS Viya before the page says anything: a delete that went through ends as one that was answered, and the item leaves the list; one that did not says A request to SAS Viya got no usable answer, and reading back what SAS Viya holds shows that it was not carried out., with the name of the button in front; where nothing can be read back, the page says that it is not known whether the request was carried out. A launch - Launch ingestion, Run test, Run optimization, Compare targets… - whose request gets no usable answer is looked for among the jobs SAS Job Execution lists as pending or running: a job of that launch is followed; where the list holds none, the page says ... the job it was to launch is not among the jobs that are running: whether it was launched is not known, as it may have ended already., and where the list cannot be read, that what SAS Viya holds could not be read back. A refusal of SAS Model Manager still says that the write failed. The lock, the buttons that are off while a write is out, a read that fails, a Delete project that stops part of the way, the bound of two minutes, a save or manifest that SAS Model Manager refuses and the ingestion run that is shown again, also after a reload, were driven against a stand-in for SAS Viya, not against SAS Viya, as were the read back of a write without an answer, every page of a listing, and the lines for a file that holds nothing the page can read.
documents.s: Pick a project and a prompt-test

documents.t: The LLM list shows every model available in your environment's LLM project. Tick each model you want to include in the comparison. When you tick one, its options appear — temperature, top-p, top-k, maximum length/tokens and any model-specific settings. Each option has an ℹ️ info icon; hover or focus it for an explanation of what the setting does and a sensible range. You can select as many models as you like; they all run against the same prompt so you get a true side-by-side comparison. Models an administrator has marked as deprecated are hidden from the list. Each option of a model is drawn as its options.json in SAS Model Manager writes it: a choice of the values of an enum with its default chosen, a box ticked by the default of a bool, and for any other option a field that holds its default - a number field for a number, unless the option's type is string, and a text field otherwise. A model whose options.json is not one the page can read is shown disabled with a note that says so. Such a file has an option that is no object with a default, or whose name holds a comma or a colon or has a blank or a quote at its ends; an enum whose values are no list of texts, hold a value with a comma or one the score code reads as something else, or do not hold its default; a bool whose default is neither true nor false (nor the text true or false); a provider key (API_KEY) whose default is no text or an empty one; another option whose default is null, a list, an object, a text with a comma or one the score code reads as something else, or a number the page writes as 1e-7 or 1e+21; or a type, label or description that is no text. The score code takes the blanks and then the quotes off the ends of a name and of a value, reads true and false in any case as true and false, and reads a text that is a number - 5, 0.50 - as that number: a text with a blank or a quote at its ends (a, say "hi"), TRUE or 5 is a text it reads as something else, while say "hi" now or it's is read as written. A number below 0.000001 or from 10^21 on with one significant digit the page writes as 1e-7 or 1e+21, which the score code reads as a text. Of API_KEY the page reads the default alone, and it does not read the label and the description of temperature, top_p, top_k and the max_* options where it draws them in number fields of its own (with a number as their default and no type enum, bool or string). Such a model is offered nowhere else on the page, not as a judge, a member or the chairman of a council or a target of a comparison or an optimization, and a saved run or an optimization run that used it does not tick it when you load it: repair the file in SAS Model Manager. The same holds for a model without its key in the credential domain. It holds as well for a model a saved run cannot keep the result of under its name - one named systemPrompt, userPrompt, author, variables, manifest, judge, mode or expected, which the page reads as fields of a run, or __proto__: its note says so, and the model has to be registered under another name to be used here. A decision model gets the same note on its card when its options.json is no object or its provider key (API_KEY) is no text or an empty one - the one field of the file the page reads. A run sends the options of a model as one text, {name:value,name:value}, which the score code splits at each comma, and each name from its value at the first colon. That is why a name holds neither and a text of options.json holds no comma, and why a run is not sent while you have typed a comma into the field of an option: the field is marked red, and the line above the Prompt Experiment Tracker names the option and its model - remove the comma and run again. A run is not sent either while the text field of an option whose default is a text holds a text the score code reads as something else - a, say "hi", TRUE or 5: the field is marked red the same way, and the line names the option and its model and says why - change the text and run again. A number in a number field is sent, and so is a number or true or false in the text field of an option whose default is a number or true or false. Any other text is sent as you typed it. An option of type string whose field is empty is not sent, and the score code uses its own default. A judge, a member or the chairman of a council is sent temperature 0 where its temperature is a number; otherwise the score code keeps its own default. This was driven against a stand-in for SAS Viya, not against SAS Viya.
documents.s: Choose the LLMs and tune their options

documents.t: The workbench has two boxes: System prompt — how the model should behave: its role, tone, task and any rules. This is the mostly-static part. User prompt — the variable input the system prompt acts on.

Real prompts rarely use fixed text. Define variables above the prompt boxes — each has a name, an optional description, a type (string or decimal) and a value — then reference them anywhere in either prompt with the {{variableName}} syntax. Right-click inside a prompt box to insert a defined variable at the cursor. When you run an experiment, the current values are filled in before the prompts are sent. Variables are more than a convenience: when you later manifest the best prompt, they become the documented inputs of the resulting model, so the model's callers know exactly what to supply.

Press Run Experiments. The tool sends the resolved prompts to every selected model in parallel and, when they return, shows each model's result in the tracker: the response (rendered as Markdown), the time to respond, and the input/output token counts. Two mechanical flags are added automatically for the run — a ⚡ icon on the fastest response and a ⌄ icon on the one with the fewest output tokens. Each response is a starting point; speed and length are not quality, which is where judging comes in.

Speed and token count do not tell you which answer is actually best. The Judge the responses section lets another LLM do that for you. Pick a judge model. A deployment can set a default, but you can always override it here. Choose a model that is not one of the ones you are comparing where possible — a model tends to over-rate its own style (self-preference bias). Optionally tick Auto-judge when the experiment finishes so judging runs by itself after every experiment, or leave it off and judge on demand. Press Judge this run on any run in the tracker. The judge sees all of the run's responses at once, in a shuffled order and under anonymous labels (so position and brand cannot sway it), reasons about them step by step, and returns a ranking. The result appears as a banner on the run: the winner, the full ranking, a confidence level, and the judge's reasoning behind a "Show reasoning" toggle. The best-ranked response also gets a 🏆 icon next to the ⚡ and ⌄ icons, and each response shows its judge rank. The judge is advisory Judging never changes your Best Response selection — that stays a decision you make. The judge rank is a signal to help you decide, alongside the responses themselves and the run metrics. Include the judge's own response. By default, if your judge model is also one of the models being compared, its own response is left out of the ranking to avoid self-preference bias. The Include the judge's own response toggle overrides that if you want it ranked anyway — its ℹ️ icon explains the trade-off. Judging needs at least two responses to compare, so if excluding the judge would leave only one, either include it or pick a different judge. What a judge call sends. Every judge call - a single judge, each member of a council and the chairman - sends the judge model's provider key, temperature 0 where its temperature is a number, and an output budget where its options.json has max_tokens or max_completion_tokens as a number. The budget is at least 4000 tokens (or the option's default, if larger) and never more than the option's maximum: a number max, or else the upper bound of its range (1 - 128000 ...). This leaves room for the judge's reasoning and its verdict even on a model defined with a small default such as max_tokens 1000, which used to end in The judge returned an unreadable verdict - and on models whose thinking counts against the limit, such as Claude 5.5. A model without such an option keeps the default of its score code. Experiment runs send what their controls hold. The judge model, the include-self setting, the auto-judge setting and the full verdict (including the reasoning) are saved with the run, so loading a run later restores everything exactly as it was judged.

Tick Best Response on the model result you consider best. This is the choice that matters: it is what a manifested model is built from and what downstream monitoring reports on. You can change it at any time. Press Save Experiments to persist the run history to the selected prompt-test in Model Manager. Saving creates a new model version, so you keep a full, auditable trail of how a prompt evolved. Open in SAS Model Manager jumps straight to the prompt's files there. If the saved runs of the prompt-test could not be read when you opened it, the page says so beside Save Experiments and in a message. Save Experiments then writes nothing, also as the first step of a manifest or an optimization, because it would replace the runs you cannot see. To read the runs, choose another entry in the list and then the prompt-test again. If the page says instead that the saved runs cannot be used, SAS Model Manager answered with a Prompt-Experiment-Tracker.json that holds no runs the page can read - a run starts with a row of its own, with a numeric runId, no model and both prompts, and goes on with at least one row per model, each model once; every field of a row is empty or of the kind the page writes there -, and opening the prompt-test again reads the same file. Save Experiments writes nothing over it either; repair or remove the file in SAS Model Manager, then choose another entry and the prompt-test again. This was driven against a stand-in for SAS Viya, not against SAS Viya. If a red line beside the button starts with Save Experiments:, a request to SAS Viya got no usable answer, and the page read back what SAS Model Manager holds: it was not carried out means that the prompt-test holds the experiments it held before; it is not known means that nothing could be read back either, and the prompt-test may hold the earlier experiments or the ones on the page. A save that was carried out and only lost its answer is a save: the page says the experiments are saved. If the line says that saving the experiments did not finish, another request to SAS Model Manager failed. The runs are still on the page in every case: press Save Experiments again before you leave it.
documents.s: Mark the best response and save

documents.t: Every run you save is listed in the tracker, newest first. For each run you can: Load it back into the workbench — prompts, variables, the selected LLMs and their options, and the judge configuration are all restored. Each option holds what the run sent: a text as it was typed, quotes and blanks inside it, backslashes and braces included, and an option of type string the run did not send - its field was empty - an empty field. That holds for a run of this session and for a saved one alike, so the run loaded sends what it sent. Delete it — the remaining runs renumber cleanly.

Once a run has a Best Response, Manifest the Best Prompt turns it into a scoreable model in SAS Model Manager, ready to be consumed elsewhere — most commonly by the Call LLM node in SAS Intelligent Decisioning. The variables you defined become the model's input variables (with their descriptions), and the prompt text is baked into the score code. Two options shape what you get: Include the LLM call in the manifested model. Off by default: the model returns the request body and endpoint (llmBody, llmURL) for the Call LLM node to execute. On: the model calls the LLM container itself and returns the response and metrics directly. Parse the LLM response into output variables. If your prompt asks the model to reply with JSON, define the output variables you expect; the model then reads each one from the response, falling back to a default, and adds a parse_status output that reports whether everything was extracted. If Finalize shows a notice that the model takes no input, the run Manifest takes - the most recent one with a ticked Best Response - uses no variable as {{name}} in either prompt (for a decision template: in the state). The inputs of a manifested model are the variables its run uses; a variable that is defined but not used does not count. Such a model is manifested without inputs (def scoreModel():, or with the provider key as its only input), and SAS Intelligent Decisioning cannot use it: SAS Model Manager answers its Python wrapper with HTTP 412 Python source code is not in the correct format. To fix it, define a variable under Define Variables, insert it into the prompt (or the state) as {{variable}}, run the experiment again, tick Best Response (or Best Decision Model) in that run and manifest. Manifest stays usable without a variable, for a model that is used outside SAS Intelligent Decisioning. If Finalize shows a warning about TLS verification, your administrator has switched off Verify TLS certificates in manifested models: a model manifested now with the included LLM call does not check the certificate of the model container it calls, and carries the tag TLS-Verification-Off in SAS Model Manager. The warning is shown before you click, for a prompt only while Include the LLM call in the manifested model is ticked — a prompt manifested for the Call LLM node makes no call itself and is not tagged. It names the option and the environment variable (LLMCONTAINERSSLVERIFY=true) that turns verification back on where the model is deployed. Manifesting the model again once the option is ticked removes the tag. The setting is meant for test systems — ask your administrator before you manifest a model that is going to production. If the line beside the manifest button starts with Not manifested or The manifest was not completed, the manifest did not go through, and no message says that the model was manifested. Not manifested means that the model still holds the score code and the tags it had before the click, and the line goes on to say why: a variable or a question of the saved run has a name the score code cannot use (rename it, run again and manifest from that run), the experiments could not be saved (the click saves them before it manifests — the line above it says what happened to the save; save the experiments, then manifest again), SAS Model Manager refused the new score code, or a request to it failed before the score code was stored — no answer at all, an error page in place of one, or a refusal of the variables, of inputVar.json or of outputVar.json. The manifest was not completed means that a request failed at the score code, or failed or was refused after it, and the line says which. When the score code of this run is stored, the requirements file (requirements.json) and the attributes of the model may be missing or still those of an earlier manifest. A request that stores the score code and gets no usable answer is read back: when the model holds the score code of this run, the manifest goes on as if it had been answered; when it does not, the line says Not manifested: the upload of the score code got no usable answer ... the model does not hold the score code of this run. Only when it cannot be read back either does the line say it is not known whether the score code of this run is stored: SAS Model Manager may have stored it, the tags of the model were not updated, and the tag TLS-Verification-Off may not match the score code the model holds until you manifest again. The button can be used again in every case. Where a request failed, manifest again; if that fails too, check the connection to SAS Viya and your permissions on the model. The same lines appear for a decision template. A line that says the tag TLS-Verification-Off could not be written, or that the tags could not be updated, is another case: the score code of this run is stored and the manifest goes on, so the message that the model was manifested can appear with it. The line asks you to put the tag right in SAS Model Manager. From here the manifested model behaves like any other model on the platform — see Deployment of Decisions for using it in a decision flow.

When your administrator has enabled prompt optimization, the flow gains an Optimize step between Build & Test and Finalize. Its Metric Guide and Optimizer Guide boxes summarise the choices next to the pickers, and a notice above Run optimization says what is still missing while the run is blocked. It closes the loop judge → optimise → judge again: instead of you rewriting the prompt by hand, DSPy searches for a better version automatically — using the runs you marked as Best Response as the examples of what a correct answer looks like. Pick the target LLM the prompt should be optimised for — or, if you are not sure which model to invest in, use Compare targets… next to the dropdown first (see Comparing target models). Choose the dataset. By default it is this prompt's experiments: every saved run with a Best Response becomes one training example — the panel shows how many usable runs you have and requires a minimum (30 by default); the responses you vouched for are treated as correct, so make sure they are. Alternatively pick a governed CAS table from the cascading server → caslib → table dropdowns — the lists come straight from CAS, so only tables that are actually loaded appear. The page lists the tables of a caslib once and keeps the list. To see a table built after that, for example with Create-Optimization-Dataset.sas in another tab, click the refresh button next to the table dropdown; it also counts the rows of the picked table again. The caslib and table pickers are type-to-filter comboboxes: click one and start typing, and the open list narrows live as you type; picking an entry (or pressing Enter on the only remaining match) selects it, and leaving the field without picking keeps your previous selection. The table needs one column per prompt variable plus a response column with the reference answer (your administrator can build one with the shipped Create-Optimization-Dataset.sas template); the panel additionally checks the table's columns and row count before launching. Choose the metric: exact match (the optimised prompt must reproduce your Best Responses, ignoring case and surrounding punctuation), token overlap (an F1 score over the words shared with the Best Response — partial credit for close answers, a good default for chatty models and longer references), or an LLM judge that sees the task and scores whether a response conveys the same answer as your Best Response, using the same rubric as the judging section (accuracy, relevance, completeness, clarity). Pick a judge that differs from the target LLM. Choose the optimizer: Bootstrap few-shot (the default — keeps your instruction and selects the strongest worked examples to teach with), MIPROv2 (additionally proposes and trials rewritten instructions, so the optimised system prompt itself can change — it makes noticeably more model calls, which the estimate reflects), or GEPA (evolves the instruction from natural-language feedback — it needs a judge model for its reflection step even when the metric is not the judge, and makes the most calls of the three). Press Run optimization. The prompt is saved first, then the work runs as a SAS job on the server — the panel shows live progress (dataset loaded, baseline scored, optimising, writing back), and a collapsible Run log tracks the job's runtime and milestones. A run makes many model calls and takes several minutes. One optimization runs at a time: you can open another prompt-test meanwhile, which then shows An optimization is already running. in place of the progress, and the prompt-test the job runs for shows the progress again when you return to it. Before its first model call the job checks that it runs as you and that it may write its result to this prompt-test; when it does not, it ends at once, and the panel says The optimization job failed. with the reason - for a compute context that does not run as you, which option your administrator has to change. The reason is the one the job wrote into its log, also when it could not record the run on the prompt-test. When the job finishes you see the metric before → after, and the run joins the prompt's Optimization history right below — every run stays on the prompt itself (no extra models are created). Expand a run to see its evolution: the baseline vs. the optimised system prompt, the few-shot examples the optimizer selected, a per-example before/after table where the answers the optimisation fixed are highlighted, and what the run spent — the model calls it made, the token totals, and an estimated cost. Load as experiment puts the optimised prompt back into the workbench with its variables and the target LLM pre-selected — run it, judge it against the original (Phase 1/2), and only manifest it if it actually wins. Like judging, optimization is advisory: it never changes your prompt or your Best Response choices by itself. Delete this optimization run removes one run from the history. If the history cannot be read from SAS Model Manager at that moment, nothing is deleted and the message says that the run was not deleted because the optimization tracker could not be read (or holds no runs the page can read). If a request of the deletion gets no usable answer, the page reads the tracker back: a tracker without the run is a deletion that went through; one that still holds it says that the tracker was not changed; only where nothing can be read back does the message say that the run may have been deleted or not. The history below is read again in every case. A history that cannot be read is no empty history: where the history stands the page says that it could not be read - choose another entry in the list and then the prompt-test again - or that SAS Model Manager answered with a file that holds no runs the page can read - an entry without its optimizationId or its status, two runs with one optimizationId, or a field of another kind than the page reads there -, and shows no run and no Delete. A finished optimization whose result cannot be read says that, not that the job failed. This was driven against a stand-in for SAS Viya, not against SAS Viya.

When is optimization useful? DSPy shines when you can say what a correct answer looks like but tinkering with the wording hasn't gotten you there: a model that answers correctly but ignores your format, a prompt that works on easy inputs and fails on edge cases, or a task where you suspect a few well-chosen worked examples would help but don't want to pick them by hand. It is not the right tool when you have only a handful of examples (the optimizer will overfit them), when no metric can meaningfully score an answer, or when the prompt already scores perfectly — there is nothing left to climb. The job guards that last case for you: if the baseline scores 1.0 on the validation split it skips the optimization phase after only the baseline calls, records the run with a note, and suggests harder examples or a stricter metric instead. Picking the metric — the metric is the optimization target, so pick the one that actually measures your task: Metric Use when Watch out for Exact match The reference is a single word or a fixed format (categories, codes, yes/no). Case and surrounding punctuation are ignored. Scores 0 for any deviation — chatty models score badly for wording alone. Token overlap Free-form text where the right answer shares its words with the reference (summaries, extractions, short explanations). Partial credit via an F1 score over shared words. Rewards word overlap, not meaning — a fluent paraphrase with different words scores low. LLM judge The reference can be said differently and still be right; meaning matters more than wording. Each scored example costs an extra judge call; pick a judge model that differs from the target. Picking the optimizer: Bootstrap few-shot (default) keeps your instruction untouched and selects worked examples (demos) that teach the model the task. It is fast, cheap and a good first run — if demos alone fix your prompt, stop there. MIPROv2 additionally rewrites the instruction itself, proposing and trialling candidates against your metric. It is the stronger tool when the instruction is the problem, at the price of many more model calls (the panel's estimate scales accordingly) — and it needs the optuna package in the compute context (admin guide). GEPA also rewrites the instruction, but reflectively instead of by blind trial: after each round, a reflection model (the judge model you pick in the panel) reads why the failing answers scored poorly and proposes a targeted improvement. With the LLM judge metric that feedback is the judge's own reasoning — the strongest combination, because the optimizer literally learns from the judge's critique; with exact match or token overlap the feedback is a generated expected-vs-produced note. GEPA selects no few-shot examples (the max-examples setting doesn't apply) and makes by far the most model calls of the three — a live 10-example run made roughly 800 calls over about half an hour — so use it when MIPROv2 plateaus or the task needs nuanced instructions. It needs no extra package: its engine ships with dspy itself. Every finished run reports what it actually spent — the model calls it made per role (target/judge), the token totals, and an estimated cost priced with the same per-token/per-second attributes as the run table — in its Optimization-history entry.
documents.s: Choosing the dataset, metric and optimizer

documents.t: Compare targets… (next to the target dropdown) answers a different question than a single optimization run: which of my deployed models should I invest in for this prompt? Pick two or more candidates in the dialog and choose one of two modes: Screen only (default) scores your current prompt on every candidate over the dataset — no optimizer runs, so it costs roughly one call per example per candidate and finishes in minutes. The result is a ranked table in the optimization history: quality (by your chosen metric), average model latency per call, calls made, and an estimated cost per candidate — best quality first, lower latency breaking ties. A candidate whose container is unreachable gets flagged instead of failing the whole comparison. Each row offers Optimize this target, which pre-selects that model in the panel so the normal single-target run continues from there. Mind the caveat: screening ranks models on the unoptimised prompt. A small model that looks weak here can improve dramatically once optimised (demos teach it the format) — treat screening as a way to weed out clearly unsuitable candidates, not as the final verdict between close ones. Also optimize each candidate runs the panel's configured optimizer on every candidate and ranks them by the optimised metric — the truthful comparison, at many times the cost (the estimate scales accordingly). Each row then shows that candidate's before → after and offers to load its optimised prompt into the workbench directly. Because this mode trains per candidate, the full minimum-sample requirement applies (screening only needs 10 examples, with a noise warning below 30). The recommended flow is both in sequence: screen first to shortlist, then sweep only the shortlist — or hand-pick the screening winner and run a normal single-target optimization on it.

The "governed CAS table" dataset source expects this schema (column names are matched case-insensitively): One column per prompt variable, named exactly like the variable in the variables manager. A prompt using {{word}} needs a column word; a prompt using {{customer}} and {{amount}} needs both columns. If the prompt has no variables, a single column userPrompt holding the full user prompt of each example. A column response with the reference answer the optimization steers toward. Rows with an empty response are skipped. For example, for a prompt with a {{word}} variable: word response hot cold big small fast slow The table must be loaded (promoted) into memory in a caslib the optimization compute context can reach — the panel's table dropdown only lists loaded tables, and the shipped Create-Optimization-Dataset.sas template builds and promotes a correctly-shaped table you can adapt. The table the program makes lives in memory only, so run the program again after a CAS restart. Two more things to know: the prompt itself (system prompt, user template, variables) still comes from the prompt's last saved run, so save at least one experiment first; and before launching, the panel validates the chosen table's columns against your prompt's variables and its row count against the sample minimum, naming exactly what is missing.

A prompt-test can also be a decision template, for the decision models your administrator registers (Jev, Von - see the Decision Definitions page). A decision model does not write text: it takes a state - a ticket, a record - and typed questions, and returns a calibrated answer per question. That inverts the design work. The state is close to a pass-through of the record, and the questions are the prompt and the output structure at once. When a decision template is the right kind. When the answer is one of a fixed set of labels, a yes/no or a level - routing, triage, screening an input, judging an output - a decision model answers in a fraction of a second and of the price of an LLM, with a probability you can gate on. It is the wrong kind for anything that must be written, computed or explained. The rules that hold for every deployment, measured on the models the framework ships: always offer a way out (an unknown or none option - without one the model invents an answer, and a threshold cannot catch it); compute in code, decide in the model (arithmetic, counting and dates fail on most decision models - pass the computed value in the state); calibrate before you set a threshold (the Evaluate step shows how far the confidence runs from the accuracy); rules own the invariants (amount limits and never-auto-deny checks belong in the ruleset of the decision flow, the model ranks and routes); no reasons come back (where a decision needs a written reason, the model triages and an LLM or a person explains the escalated cases); and route the uncertain slice to a person or an LLM - that hybrid matched or beat the LLM alone at a fraction of the cost in independent studies. The Prompt Builder keeps the same steps and the same governance (project, prompt-test, tracker, manifest) and swaps the pieces that differ: Setup: the card starts with the question What are you building? - a prompt template for LLMs, a decision template for decision models, or a RAG setup - with a sentence on each. A kind your administrator has switched off is not among the cards, and with a single kind left the question is not shown. Each view lists its own projects and prompt-tests: a project created in the decision view is made for decision templates (it carries the Decision-Engineering tag beside Prompt-Engineering), and every project from before holds LLM prompts and stays in the LLM view. The kind is stored with the project and with the prompt-test, so both open as what they are every time. The model list on Build & Test then shows the decision models instead of the LLMs, and the judge card disappears - there is nothing to judge. Build & Test: instead of two prompts you write a state template (text or JSON, with {{variables}} inserted like in a prompt) and design the questions: a name (it becomes an output of the manifested model), a type, instructions, and the options of a choice (key: description, one per line) or the levels of a score (lowest first). A yes/no noul needs nothing more. You can start from a template - ticket routing, an agent guardrail, a prompt-injection screen, claims triage, complaint classification, an LLM-as-a-judge, RAG chunk relevance, an out-of-scope check - and change it; every field has a ? that explains what it does and what was measured. Give a question an expected answer for the current variable values and the run is checked for you: a run has one Best Decision Model (German Bestes Entscheidungsmodell) - the decision-template reading of Best Response: your choice of the best decision model of that run. The page ticks the first result of the run whose answers all match; every result whose answers all match carries the note All expected answers matched. You can still change the tick: ticking another result of the run unticks the one ticked before - also a result whose answers did not match, which then carries no note. Manifest takes the Best Decision Model of the most recent run that has one. A run saved with more than one ticked box shows the first, the one Manifest took. This was driven against a stand-in for SAS Viya, not against SAS Viya. The designer checks your questions as you type. Things to fix (no name, no instructions, fewer than two options) block the run; warnings and tips do not, but read them: a choice without an escape option (unknown, none) makes the model invent an answer when the text fits nothing - in the measurements behind this guidance Jev put 0.88 on an invented answer, and a confidence threshold does not catch that - so a new choice starts with unknown and a one-click fix adds it to an existing one. Instructions that ask the model to calculate, count or compare dates fail on most decision models (compute the value in your code and put it in the state), asking why gets no answer (decision models return no reasons), and extraction is not what they do. A checklist under the questions sums it up, and the state shows its token estimate. The model cards say what each decision model is and takes - provider, licence, context, option limit, question types, the price of the current request per thousand calls - and whether it fits the request. A model that cannot take it (a score question on a choice-only model, more options than it accepts) is skipped by the run and named, not failed. The tracker reads every answer for you: one sentence on how sure the model was (a clear decision, a preference, a close call, an abstention) and a badge saying what a flow gated at the default threshold would do - automate, escalate, or abstained when the model chose the escape option. A confident choice from a question without an escape option is flagged as possibly invented. Each model's probability per option or level is drawn beside it, and when several models answered one run their top answers stand side by side, marked all agree or models disagree - disagreement means the input is ambiguous or the options overlap. Evaluate (step 3): a decision model cannot be read like a response, so it is measured on cases with a known answer. Use the saved runs that carry expected answers, or a CAS table with one column per variable and an expected_<question> column per question; every row is one call per selected model. You get the accuracy per question (abstentions counted apart), a confusion table for choices (rows: expected, columns: answered), the confidence threshold trade-off - move the slider and read how many cases stay automatic at that threshold (coverage) and how often those are right - and the calibration: the expected calibration error, the Brier score and a reliability diagram of accuracy per confidence bin against the diagonal. Read the calibration before you set the threshold: a threshold on a confidence that runs ahead of the accuracy automates mistakes. That threshold is the number your decision flow branches on - cases below it go to a person or an LLM. The numbers are those of the answers: a case the model gave no answer to - its call failed - is counted apart as not answered, never as a wrong answer, and it is never automated. A model that answered none of the cases shows no answers to score for each question in place of the numbers, and where no case stays automatic at a threshold, or no answer is scored for the calibration, a dash stands in place of the number. The first read of the rows of a CAS table is sent to the sign-in of SAS Viya, and the browser can lose it on the way; the page then reads them once more, so the first click of Evaluate works. If the rows cannot be read all the same, the line under Evaluate names the table and the reason. This was driven against a stand-in for SAS Viya, not against SAS Viya. Finalize: the manifested model takes the state template's variables as inputs, bakes the questions in, calls the decision model itself, and returns one typed pair per question - <name> (the chosen option, yes/no, or the level number) and <name>_confidence - beside the whole answer map, the first question's headline answer and confidence, and the call's time and token count. No JSON parsing, no parse_status. Finalize shows Manifest the Best Decision Model; its button Manifest Best Decision Model takes the Best Decision Model of the most recent run that has one and stays off, with the hint You have to select a Best Decision Model using the checkboxes., while no box is ticked. A decision template always calls its model itself, so the warning about TLS verification applies to it whenever your administrator has switched verification off. A state that uses no {{variable}} gives a model without inputs, which SAS Intelligent Decisioning cannot use; Finalize then shows the notice about a model that takes no input. After an upgrade from release 2.2.0. Manifest every decision template that was manifested with 2.2.0 again: open it, go to Finalize and manifest. The score code release 2.2.0 wrote for a decision template is not valid Python, so such a model cannot be scored; the manifest of the current release writes it anew. A question whose name the designer now refuses has to be renamed first.

The third kind on the Setup card is a RAG setup for a document collection, and it is not a prompt at all. A RAG setup is one folder of documents wired to one collection in a vector store, together with everything that decides how the documents get there: which embedding model turns text into vectors, how the text is cut into chunks, whether a prompt enriches each chunk, and where the pipeline keeps its tables. Saved, it is a governed model in SAS Model Manager, as a prompt-test is. Manifested, it becomes an ingestion job that keeps the collection current and a retrieval model a decision can call. This part of the Prompt Builder is called the RAG Builder. What retrieval-augmented generation is, and what the pipeline does with your documents, is the subject of the RAG guide. This section is about the screen. Choosing the kind swaps the steps. A RAG setup has nothing to run an experiment on, so it does not reuse the prompt steps: choosing it replaces them in the stepper with four steps of its own. The same question, What are you building?, sits at the top of the RAG Builder's Setup card and takes you back. Step What you do there 1 Setup Pick or create a RAG project and a RAG setup inside it — a project groups related setups, a setup is one document corpus wired to one collection. Write its documentation here too: what the corpus is, what it should be used for and where its limits are. It is saved onto the model, so a governance review reads your own caveats. 2 Documents & chunks Name the document folder, choose the embedding model from the ones registered in your environment, set the chunking, and optionally add enrichment — prompts called once per chunk. The embedding model comes before the chunking because its token window caps the chunk size. 3 Store & output Choose the vector database and the collection, the caslib and prefix of the pipeline tables, and the folder for the generated artifacts. Save setup stores the settings of every step in SAS Model Manager. Manifest setup saves too, then generates the ingestion job, the SAS Studio flow and the retrieval model. 4 Run & test Launch ingestion runs the manifested job against the document folder and reports its milestones. The run belongs to its setup: with another setup open the card is not shown, and it is back when you open this setup again - after a reload of the page only while its job is still pending or running. A run in which some documents could not be ingested still ends as completed, with a warning that counts them — the other documents are in the collection. Browse ledger lists every document the pipeline has seen, with its status and chunk count. Test retrieval asks the live collection a question and shows the chunks that come back — the quickest way to tell whether the chunk size and the embedding model suit the corpus. Launching and testing need a manifested setup. As in the prompt flow, any step opens at any time and none is ticked off. Steps 2 to 4 show their settings once a setup is selected in step 1. If Manifest setup shows a warning about TLS verification, your administrator has switched off Verify TLS certificates in manifested models: the retrieval model registered then does not check the certificate of the embedding container it calls, and carries the tag TLS-Verification-Off in SAS Model Manager. The warning is shown before you click and names the option and the two environment variables (RAGEMBED_SSLVERIFY=true, RAGSTORE_SSLVERIFY=true) that turn verification back on where the model is deployed. The ingestion and Test retrieval are not affected. Deleting a setup or a project. Delete setup and Delete project, on the Setup step, remove the setup, or the project with every setup in it, from SAS Model Manager. A decision in SAS Intelligent Decisioning that calls the retrieval model of a setup stops working when the setup is gone, so before the page asks you to confirm it looks up which decisions still reference the setup and puts the answer into the dialog. The note names the decisions that use the setup and will break, each with a link to the decision — for a project it does so setup by setup. Otherwise it says that no decision references the setup, or that this could not be checked, in which case a decision may still depend on it. Read the note before you confirm: SAS Model Manager deletes a setup that a decision still uses without objecting. The decision itself stays; in SAS Intelligent Decisioning its model node then carries an error badge, and Validate fails with NOT_FOUND for each model that was deleted. The vector-store collection and its CAS tables are not touched: the data stays where it is, and what goes is the record of what built it. Switching between kinds keeps each side's state. The prompt side and the RAG side are both kept while the report is open; the one you are not looking at is only hidden. Go from a prompt template to a RAG setup and back, and the project, the prompt-test, the prompts you typed and the tracker are as you left them — and so are the RAG project, the setup and the settings you have not saved yet. What is running keeps running: an ingestion goes on reporting its milestones while you work on a prompt, and an experiment or an optimization finishes while you look at a setup. After a switch you are on the Setup step of the side you chose. Two details about switching: The first time you choose the RAG setup in a session, the RAG Builder is loaded and its card shows Loading… for a moment. If that fails, the page stays where it was and the reason appears under the cards; choosing the card again retries. A change between the two template kinds — from a prompt template to a decision template or back — is refused with a message while an experiment or an optimization is running, because both use the same workbench. Going to the RAG setup and back is never refused. If the card is missing or cannot be chosen. Whether RAG setups are offered is a setting of the report, made by your administrator. Where it is switched off there is no RAG card. Where the card is shown but greyed out, it says why — RAG needs a credential domain to reach the vector store, and the report is set up without one. Where the two kinds meet. The enrichment prompts of step 2 are prompt templates. Build and judge one in the prompt flow, manifest it on Finalize with Include the LLM call in the manifested model and Parse the LLM response into output variables switched on, and it can be picked in a RAG setup's enrichment section: one of its outputs becomes the context header that is embedded with each chunk, the others become columns you can filter on. The administration guide says what that costs and what to check before you turn it on. A setup can show its vector database as not offered for new setups. Your administrator has stopped offering that database for new work; the setup keeps it and can still be saved, launched and tested.

Everything you save lands in Model Manager as a Prompt-Experiment-Tracker.json on the prompt-test. Administrators can roll all of it up into a single PROMPT_EXPERIMENTS table for Visual Analytics reporting — including the option values used, the per-run metrics, your best-response choices and the judge's verdict (rank, chosen model and confidence). The tracker files are the source of truth; the report is a convenience view over them.
documents.s: Where your experiments show up for reporting

documents.t: Hosted models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, …) need an API key. Keys are not typed into the tool or the URL — they are resolved from a SAS Viya credential domain under your own identity (a personal credential, or one your group holds), so they never end up in a shareable link and who may run paid model calls is an identity decision. A model you hold no key for is shown disabled with a note naming the missing entry; ask your administrator to add it. See Managing Credentials for the details.
